bank.why: Vernation (not venation!) = leaves within the bud.

bank.q: Leaves arranged in a cluster on a very short, stumpy stem on top of the root, as in radish.
bank.why: Radical = at the root top; cauline = on a stem with internodes.

bank.q: The three main types of cauline phyllotaxy are...
bank.why: Cauline: alternate, opposite, whorled.

bank.q: Only a single leaf on each node, the leaves taking turns along the stem.
bank.why: Alternate = 1 per node.

bank.q: Alternate leaves arranged in two vertical rows on the two sides of the stem (Annona, grasses).
bank.why: Di = two rows.

bank.q: Alternate leaves arranged in three rows, as in Cyperus.
bank.why: Tri = three rows.

bank.q: Alternate leaves arranged spirally around the stem, as in Hibiscus.
bank.why: Spiral alternate: Hibiscus.

bank.q: A pair of leaves arranged oppositely on each node.
bank.why: Opposite = 2 per node.

bank.q: Opposite phyllotaxy in which adjacent pairs are at right angles to each other (Ixora, Calotropis).
bank.why: Decussate = crossed at right angles.

bank.q: Opposite phyllotaxy in which adjacent pairs are exactly one above the other in the same plane (Quisqualis).
bank.why: Superposed = stacked directly above.

bank.q: Three or more leaves arising from each node in a circle around the stem (Nerium, Alstonia).
bank.why: Whorled = 3+ per node.

bank.q: Leaves are modified in different ways for...
bank.why: Tendrils, hooks, spines, scales, pitchers, phyllodes.

bank.q: Long, spirally coiled, spring-like leaves that help weak-stemmed plants climb.
bank.why: Leaf tendrils are sensitive to contact (Pisum, Gloriosa, Lathyrus).

bank.q: In Pisum, leaf tendrils are...
bank.why: Pisum: tendrils are modified terminal leaflets.

bank.q: In Gloriosa, leaf tendrils are...
bank.why: Gloriosa: tendrils are modified leaf tips.

bank.q: In Lathyrus (sweet pea), leaf tendrils are...
bank.why: Lathyrus (sweet pea): tendrils are entire leaves.

bank.q: In Clematis, leaf tendrils are...
bank.why: Clematis: tendrils are modified rachillae.

bank.q: Hook-like modifications of the terminal leaflets for clinging, as in Bignonia unguis-cati.
bank.why: Three terminal leaflets become cat-claw hooks.

bank.q: Sharply pointed leaf modifications characteristic of xerophytes like cacti.
bank.why: Spines: defense, protection and control of transpiration.

bank.q: In Ananas (pineapple) and Agave, leaf spines are modified...
bank.why: Opuntia: minute leaves of axillary buds; Ananas/Agave: leaf margins.

bank.q: Thin, stalkless, membranous leaves that protect the axillary buds in their axils.
bank.why: In onion they are fleshy, storing water, mucilage and food.

bank.q: A flask-shaped modification of the leaf lamina for trapping insects (Nepenthes, Sarracenia).
bank.why: Insectivorous plants trap insects in pitchers.

bank.q: In Nepenthes, the lid covering the mouth of the pitcher is the...
bank.why: The operculum is a modified part of the leaf tip.

bank.q: In Nepenthes, which part of the leaf is modified into the pitcher?
bank.why: The lamina becomes the pitcher; the petiole is flat and tendril-like.

bank.q: A flat, leaf-like, photosynthetic modification of the petiole or rachis.
bank.why: Phyllodes are xerophytic adaptations (Acacia, Parkinsonia).

bank.q: A phyllode is a ___ modification, while a phylloclade is a ___ modification.
bank.why: Phyllode = petiole/rachis; phylloclade = stem.

bank.q: Which describes a phyllode, not a phylloclade?
bank.a: Unbranched, no nodes and internodes, never succulent
bank.why: Phyllodes lack nodes; phylloclades have them and are succulent.

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the functions of leaves listed?
d: Help in pollination by attractive coloration
bank.why: Anchorage is a root function.

bank.q: In a plant mutant, every leaf grows from the same side of the stem and the lower leaves are heavily shaded. What is most likely affected?
bank.why: Phyllotaxy arranges leaves to provide sufficient light.

bank.q: A Nepenthes plant's pitchers trap insects, but the insects are never digested and the plant lacks nitrogen. What is most likely not working?
bank.a: Enzyme secretion by the pitcher wall
bank.why: Insects are digested by enzymes secreted by the pitcher wall.

bank.q: Insects slip into a pitcher but many escape before being digested. Which part is most likely not closing?
bank.why: The operculum closes the mouth to prevent escape.

bank.q: An Australian Acacia loses its leaflets early, yet keeps photosynthesizing with flat structures, saving water. What are they?
bank.why: In Acacia, the rachis flattens into a leaf-like phyllode.

bank.q: A pea plant's leaves photosynthesize normally, but the plant cannot climb its support. Which leaf part is most likely affected?
bank.why: In Pisum, the terminal leaflets become tendrils.

bank.q: Spines are removed from a group of cacti in a dry field. Compared with untouched cacti, what would you most likely observe?
bank.a: More grazing damage and more water loss
d: Faster photosynthesis and no other change
bank.why: Leaf spines defend, protect and control transpiration.

bank.q: A researcher wants to test whether leaf arrangement affects how much light lower leaves receive. Which design is most appropriate?
bank.a: Grow plants of one species with the same height and leaf number, measure light at the lower leaves under one lamp, and compare with plants whose leaves were made to overlap
d: Grow plants of one species with the same height and leaf number, measure light at their lower leaves under one lamp, with no repositioned group
Grow plants of different species, measure light at their lower leaves under one lamp, and compare with plants whose leaves overlap
Grow plants of one species, measure light at the lower leaves of one plant under a lamp and another in sunlight, and compare
bank.why: Same species, size and light source keep everything constant except the arrangement; repeats make the result reliable.
bank.hint: Same plant, change only the arrangement.

bank.term: Leaves keep growing but stem doesn't
bank.q: A corn plant keeps producing new leaves at its shoot tip, but its internodes stay very short. Which meristem is most likely affected?
bank.why: Intercalary meristems at the base of internodes lengthen them; the apical meristem (new leaves) is fine.

bank.q: A tree's trunk shows no new growth rings for several years, though the tree grows taller and has leaves. Which tissue is most likely inactive?
bank.why: Growth rings come from secondary xylem made by the vascular cambium.

bank.q: A root's apical meristem makes new root tissue toward the base, but worn-out root cap cells are never replaced. Which initials are most likely defective?
bank.why: Toward the apex, the meristem forms the calyptrogen, which makes the root cap.

bank.q: A potato tuber forms but stores almost no starch, though its outer skin and vascular tissue are normal. Which cells are most likely affected?
bank.why: Parenchyma stores food and water in stems, roots, seeds and fruits.

bank.q: A walnut variety has a soft, easily crushed shell, though the seed inside is healthy. Which cells are most likely lacking?
bank.why: Sclereids make structures like nut shells rock-hard.

bank.q: Rice plants in a flooded field have healthy leaves, but their submerged roots run short of oxygen. Which tissue normally moves oxygen down to them?
bank.why: Aerenchyma's air spaces carry oxygen to submerged parts and give buoyancy.

bank.q: A leaf has a healthy cuticle and its guard cells have chloroplasts, but the guard cells never become turgid. What happens to gas exchange?
bank.a: The stomata stay closed, so CO2 cannot enter
d: The stomata stay wide open, so water is lost
The cuticle is lost, so the leaf dries out
The xylem stops forming, so water can't come in
bank.why: Turgid guard cells open the stoma; without turgor it stays closed.

bank.q: A cork layer covers a woody stem completely with no lenticels. What is the most likely problem?
bank.a: Inner living tissues cannot exchange gases
d: The stem loses too much water
bank.why: Cork is nearly gas-tight; lenticels allow gas exchange.

bank.q: Why would a thick cuticle on root hairs be harmful?
d: It would make the roots grow upward
It would dissolve the root cap
bank.why: The cuticle prevents water movement, so root hairs lack it in order to absorb water.

bank.term: Water but no minerals reach leaves
bank.q: A plant's leaves get water but show mineral deficiency, though the soil is rich in minerals and the roots are healthy. Which tissue carries both water and minerals upward?
bank.why: Xylem conducts water and minerals from the root to the rest of the plant.

bank.q: A tomato plant's leaves photosynthesize normally, but its fruits stay small and unsweet. Which tissue is most likely failing to deliver sugar?
bank.why: Phloem carries sugar from sources (leaves) to sinks (fruits).

bank.q: Sugar is loaded into a plant's sieve tubes but cannot pass from one sieve-tube element to the next. Which structure is most likely blocked?
bank.why: Sieve plates are the porous end walls between sieve-tube elements.

bank.q: In a flowering plant, the perforation plates of the vessels become blocked. Water transport continues slowly. Which cells are most likely still carrying it?
bank.why: Tracheids move water through pits; they are slower than vessels.

bank.q: A dicot seedling forms many thin roots from its stem base but no single main root. What most likely happened?
bank.a: The radicle failed to develop into a tap root
d: The root cap was too large
bank.why: Tap roots develop from the radicle; without it, adventitious roots take over.

bank.q: A root grows long quickly, but its epidermal cells never form hair-like outgrowths. What will the plant most likely suffer from?
d: No cell division at the tip
bank.why: Root hairs give the main absorptive surface.

bank.q: A root has a complete root cap but no new cells are formed behind it. Which zone is not working?
bank.why: The meristematic zone (growing point) is the zone of cell division.

bank.q: A dahlia's fasciculated root stores plenty of inulin but no new shoot grows from it. Which explains this?
bank.a: It was separated without a stem portion carrying a bud
d: It stores too much starch for a bud to form on it
It is really a modified stem, not a root
It lost its root cap when it was dug up
bank.why: A dahlia root needs part of the stem crown with a bud to sprout.

bank.q: A carrot plant grows leaves normally but its main root stays thin. Which function of the root is most likely impaired?
bank.a: Food storage in the tap root
bank.why: In carrots, the tap root swells to store reserve food (conical).

bank.q: A Cuscuta (dodder) vine wraps around a host plant but slowly dies. What is most likely not working?
bank.a: Its roots that absorb food from the host (haustoria)
d: Its root hairs that absorb water from the soil
Its pneumatophores that take in air for the roots
Its velamen that absorbs moisture from the air
bank.why: Cuscuta absorbs food from the host through specialized roots.

bank.q: Mangrove seeds that fall and germinate in the water drown, unlike seedlings that had already germinated on the parent. Which adaptation helps mangrove seedlings survive?
bank.why: Vivipary: seeds germinate while still attached to the parent.

bank.q: Orchid seedlings in sterile medium fail to absorb nutrients well compared with those in natural soil. What is most likely missing?
bank.why: Orchids have endotrophic mycorrhiza (fungus inside cortex cells).

bank.q: In autumn, a tree drops its leaves but its axillary buds remain. Where on the twig is each bud found?
bank.a: Above the leaf scar, in the former leaf axil
d: In the middle of the internode
bank.why: Axillary buds sit in leaf axils, just above where the leaf scar forms.

bank.q: A gardener removes the terminal bud of a plant, but no lateral branches appear. What is the most likely explanation?
bank.a: The axillary buds were damaged or absent
d: The plant produced more auxin at the tip
bank.why: Without the tip, lateral buds should grow; if they don't, the buds themselves are the problem.

bank.q: A garlic bulb grows its main shoot normally but forms no cloves. Which buds are most likely not developing?
bank.why: Daughter bulbs (cloves) form from axillary buds.

bank.q: After the dry season, a Colocasia plant fails to regrow even though its corm is present. The corm is found shrunken and empty. What most likely happened?
bank.a: Its stored food was used up and no new corm formed
d: Its tunic was damaged, so it dried out
Its eyes were removed before planting
It changed into a rhizome underground
bank.why: Each season the old corm's food feeds the new shoot, which forms a new corm.

bank.q: A strawberry runner's daughter plant dies after the runner is cut, while others survive. What did it most likely lack?
bank.a: Its own adventitious roots at the node
d: A terminal bud on the mother
bank.why: Rooted daughter plants can live independently once separated.

bank.q: An Agave plant's flowering stalk forms flowers, but no plantlets fall from it. What normally forms these plantlets?
bank.why: In Agave, floral buds become bulbils.

bank.q: A grass leaf blade flops away from the stem because the part wrapping the stem is torn. Which part was torn?
bank.why: Monocot leaf bases form a sheath that encircles the stem.

bank.q: A banana's trunk-like structure is cut and found to be made of tightly overlapping layers. What is it?
bank.a: A pseudostem of sheathing leaf bases
d: A woody stem with growth rings
A phylloclade, a flat green stem
bank.why: Banana's overlapping leaf sheaths form the pseudostem.

bank.q: On a neem branch, each leaflet falls off on its own, but no buds are left in their axils. This supports that neem leaves are...
bank.why: Leaflets lack axillary buds; this is a compound leaf.

bank.q: A Bignonia unguis-cati vine cannot cling to a wall, though its other leaves are healthy. Which structures are most likely damaged?
bank.why: Its three terminal leaflets form cat-claw hooks.

bank.q: In an onion, the axillary buds dry out because the leaves around them are missing. Which leaves normally protect them?
bank.why: Scale leaves protect the axillary buds in their axils.

bank.q: Insects visit a Nepenthes pitcher but rarely fall in. Which feature is most likely missing?
bank.a: The sugary secretion that makes the rim slippery
bank.why: A sugary secretion makes the rim slippery so insects slip in.

bank.q: The same Limnophila plant has dissected leaves underwater and entire leaves in the air. What does this show?
bank.a: Leaf form can change with environment on one plant (heterophylly)
d: Two different species are growing together
Phyllotaxy changed from alternate to whorled
bank.why: Heterophylly: different kinds of leaves on the same plant.

bank.q: A researcher wants to show that grass regrows from the base of its leaves, not from the tip. Which design is best?
bank.a: Cut the tips off some grass blades and the bases off others, leave some uncut as controls, keep light and water equal, and measure regrowth over a week
d: Cut the tips off all the grass blades, keep light and water equal, and measure how much each blade regrows over a week
Cut the tips off some blades and the bases off others, give the tip-cut group more water, and measure regrowth over a week
Cut the tips off some blades and the bases off others, leave some uncut, and look at them once the next morning
bank.why: Comparing tip-cut, base-cut and uncut blades isolates where growth comes from.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A student wants to test whether air spaces help water-plant stems float. What is the best approach?
bank.a: Take equal pieces of the same stem, remove the air from some by vacuum while leaving others untreated as controls, and compare whether they float in the same water
d: Remove the air by vacuum from all the stem pieces, then put them in water and record which ones float
Take a piece of water-plant stem and a piece of tree branch and compare whether each floats in the same water
Remove the air from some pieces, leave others untreated, and put the two groups in different containers of water
bank.why: Only the air content differs between treated and control pieces.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.term: Experiment: do guard cells control stomata?
bank.q: A researcher wants to test whether water uptake by guard cells opens stomata. Which design is most appropriate?
bank.a: Peel epidermis strips from the same leaf, place some in plain water and others in a strong salt solution, keep light the same, and compare stomatal opening under a microscope
d: Peel epidermis strips from the same leaf, place all of them in plain water under the same light, and look at stomatal opening
Peel strips from two different species, put one in plain water and the other in salt solution, and compare stomatal opening
Peel strips from the same leaf, place some in plain water in the light and others in salt solution in the dark, and compare
bank.why: Salt solution draws water out of guard cells; plain water keeps them turgid; everything else is the same.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A student wants to show that lenticels let gases into a woody twig. What is the best method?
bank.a: Seal the lenticels of some twigs with petroleum jelly and leave others unsealed as controls, place both in sealed jars with a CO2 indicator, and compare the change
d: Seal the lenticels of all the twigs with petroleum jelly, place them in sealed jars with a CO2 indicator, and record the change
Seal the lenticels of some twigs and leave others unsealed, but put only the sealed twigs in jars with a CO2 indicator
Peel off the bark of some twigs and seal the leaves of others, then place both in jars with a CO2 indicator
bank.why: Only sealing the lenticels differs, so any difference in gas exchange is due to them.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A researcher wants to show that water vapor leaves a plant through its leaves. Which setup is best?
bank.a: Cover a leafy shoot with a clear plastic bag and a leafless shoot of the same plant with another bag (control), keep both in the same light, and compare the water collected
d: Cover a leafy shoot with a clear plastic bag, keep it in the light for a day, and record whether water collects inside
Cover a leafy shoot with a bag in the light and a leafless shoot with a bag in the dark, then compare the water collected
Cover the pot and soil of the plant with plastic and leave the shoot uncovered, then check for water the next day
bank.why: Only the presence of leaves differs; droplets collect where transpiration happens.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A student wants to identify which tissue carries water. What should they do?
bank.a: Place freshly cut stems in dyed water alongside stems in plain water, then cut thin cross-sections and see which tissue is stained
d: Place freshly cut stems in dyed water, then cut thin cross-sections after some hours and see which tissue is stained
Place stems in dyed water alongside stems in plain water, but look only at the outside of the stems without cutting
Place stems of one plant in dyed water and stems of another species in plain water, then compare cross-sections
bank.why: Dye follows the water path (xylem); plain-water stems are the control.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A researcher wants to show that sieve tubes depend on companion cells. What is the best design?
bank.a: In identical stems, destroy the companion cells along one region while leaving neighboring sieve tubes untouched as controls, then compare sugar flow through both
d: In identical stems, destroy the companion cells along one region of every stem, then measure sugar flow through it
Destroy the companion cells in one stem and the sieve tubes in another, then compare the sugar flow in both
Destroy the companion cells along one region and compare sugar flow with a stem from a different species
bank.why: Only the companion cells are removed; untouched sieve tubes serve as the control.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A researcher wants to test whether roots respond to gravity and to water. What are the most appropriate steps?
bank.a: Grow seedlings in the dark; rotate some on a clinostat beside unrotated controls, then in a separate trial put a damp cloth on one side, and record root bending
d: Grow seedlings in sunlight, rotate some on a clinostat beside unrotated controls, add a damp cloth on one side, and record root bending
Grow seedlings in the dark, rotate them on a clinostat and add a damp cloth in the same trial, and record root bending
Grow seedlings in the dark, rotate all of them on a clinostat with no controls, then add a damp cloth and record root bending
bank.why: Each stimulus is tested alone (light excluded throughout): rotation removes gravity, the damp cloth adds moisture on one side.
bank.hint: One stimulus at a time; exclude light.

bank.q: Following a hydrotropism study, a researcher now wants to test light alone. Which keeps the other variables constant?
bank.a: Grow seedlings in moist, uniform medium with gravity unchanged, illuminate some from one side and keep others in darkness as controls, then compare root direction
d: Grow seedlings in moist medium, light them from one side only, and record the direction of root growth with no dark group
Grow seedlings in moist medium, light some from one side and keep others dark, but rotate only the lit ones on a clinostat
Grow lit seedlings in wet soil and dark seedlings in dry soil, with gravity unchanged, and compare root direction
bank.why: Moisture and gravity are equal for both groups; only light differs.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A researcher wants to show that the root cap is needed to sense gravity. Which design is best?
bank.a: Carefully remove the root caps from some seedlings and keep others intact as controls, lay all roots horizontally in the dark under the same moisture, and see which bend downward
d: Remove the root caps from all the seedlings, lay the roots horizontally in the dark, and record which ones bend downward
Remove the root caps from some seedlings and keep others intact, but lay only the capless roots horizontally, and see which bend
Remove the root caps from some seedlings kept in light and leave others intact in the dark, then see which bend downward
bank.why: Only the root cap differs; intact roots bend down, decapped ones do not until the cap regrows.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A student wants to test whether root hairs increase water absorption. Which design is best?
bank.a: Use seedlings of the same age, gently remove the root hairs from some and keep others intact, give all the same volume of water in sealed containers, and measure the water taken up
d: Use seedlings of the same age, remove the root hairs from all of them, give each the same water, and measure the water taken up
Remove the root hairs from some seedlings and keep others intact, but give the hairless ones more water, and measure the uptake
Remove the root hairs from one seedling and keep another intact, and see which looks more wilted after a day
bank.why: Only the root hairs differ; water uptake is measured directly.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A student wants to find which root zone absorbs the most water. What is the best approach?
bank.a: Expose only one zone at a time to dyed water while sealing the rest of the root in wax, repeat for each zone with identical seedlings, and compare dye uptake
d: Put the whole root in dyed water for some hours, then cut sections along it and see which zone took up the most dye
Expose one zone of one seedling to dyed water while sealing the rest in wax, and record how much dye it takes up
Expose the root tip of one seedling and the root hair zone of a different species to dyed water, and compare uptake
bank.why: Testing one zone at a time while sealing the others isolates where absorption happens.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A researcher wants to show that root nodules supply nitrogen to pea plants. What is the best design?
bank.a: Grow peas in nitrogen-free sand, inoculate some with Rhizobium and leave others uninoculated as controls, keep everything else the same, and compare growth and nodule formation
d: Grow peas in nitrogen-free sand, inoculate all of them with Rhizobium, keep everything the same, and record growth and nodules
Grow peas in nitrogen-free sand and inoculate some with Rhizobium, but add nitrogen fertilizer to the uninoculated ones, and compare
Grow peas in rich garden soil, inoculate some with Rhizobium and leave others uninoculated, and compare their growth
bank.why: Nitrogen-free sand means the only nitrogen source differs between groups.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A researcher wants to test whether Vanda's aerial roots absorb moisture from the air. Which design is best?
bank.a: Keep identical orchids in humid chambers, coat the aerial roots of some with a waterproof layer and leave others uncoated, water none of them at the base, and compare their water content
d: Keep identical orchids in humid chambers, coat the aerial roots of all of them, water none at the base, and measure their water content
Coat the aerial roots of some orchids and leave others uncoated, but water the uncoated ones at the base, and compare water content
Coat the aerial roots of some orchids in a humid chamber and leave others uncoated in dry air, then compare water content
bank.why: With no soil water, only the roots' contact with humid air differs.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A researcher wants to show that mycorrhizal fungi improve phosphate uptake. What is the best design?
bank.a: Grow identical seedlings in sterilized low-phosphate soil, add mycorrhizal fungi to half and not to the other half, keep conditions the same, and measure phosphate in the plants
d: Grow identical seedlings in sterilized low-phosphate soil, add mycorrhizal fungi to all of them, and measure phosphate in the plants
Add mycorrhizal fungi to half the seedlings and phosphate fertilizer to the other half, then measure phosphate in the plants
Grow one seedling with mycorrhizal fungi in a forest and one without in a pot, then measure phosphate in each
bank.why: Same soil, light and water; only the fungus differs.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: In an apical dominance experiment, which control group is essential?
bank.a: Intact plants with the terminal bud left on, grown under the same conditions
d: Plants of a different species, with the terminal bud left on
Plants grown under brighter light, with the terminal bud removed
Plants with all the leaves removed, grown under the same conditions
bank.why: The intact group shows normal apical dominance to compare against.

bank.q: A researcher wants to test whether shoots grow toward light. Which design is best?
bank.a: Grow identical seedlings, light some from one side only and others from directly above, keep water and temperature equal, and compare stem bending
d: Grow identical seedlings with light from one side only, keep water and temperature equal, and record how much the stems bend
Light some seedlings from one side and others from above, but water the side-lit ones more, and compare stem bending
Light one seedling from the side and another from above, and compare their heights after a week
bank.why: Only the direction of light differs.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A researcher wants to know whether a ginger rhizome piece needs a bud to grow. What is the best approach?
bank.a: Cut rhizome pieces of equal size, some with a bud and some without, plant all under the same conditions, and record which produce shoots
d: Cut rhizome pieces of equal size, all with a bud, plant them under the same conditions, and record which produce shoots
Cut pieces with and without a bud, plant those with a bud in moist soil and the rest in dry soil, and record shoots
Cut one piece with a bud and one without, of different sizes, plant them, and record which produces shoots
bank.why: Bud vs no bud is the only difference.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.term: Experiment: where food is stored in onion
bank.q: A student wants to show that an onion stores food in its fleshy leaves, not in its disc-like stem. What is the best approach?
bank.a: Separate the fleshy scale leaves and the basal disc, test equal masses of each with the same sugar or starch test, and compare the results
d: Test the whole onion with a sugar test, then compare the result with a potato tested the same way
Separate the scale leaves and the basal disc, test the leaves for sugar and the disc for starch, and compare the results
Separate the scale leaves and the disc, test a large mass of leaves and a tiny piece of disc, and compare the results
bank.why: Testing each part separately with the same test shows where the food is.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A researcher wants to test whether tendrils coil because of touch. Which design is best?
bank.a: Gently stroke one side of some tendrils with a rod and leave others untouched as controls, keep light and water the same, and observe coiling over hours
d: Gently stroke one side of all the tendrils with a rod, keep light and water the same, and observe coiling over hours
Stroke some tendrils and leave others untouched, but shine extra light on the stroked ones, and observe coiling
Stroke one tendril and leave one untouched, and observe them for a few seconds
bank.why: Touch is the only variable; untouched tendrils are the control.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A student wants to show that the green pads of Opuntia photosynthesize. What is the best approach?
bank.a: Cover some pads with foil and leave others exposed (control) on the same plant, then after a few days test both for starch
d: Cover all the pads with foil for a few days, then test them for starch
Cover some pads with foil on one plant and leave others exposed on another species, then test for starch
Cover some pads with foil and leave others exposed, then test only the exposed pads for starch
bank.why: Light is the only difference between covered and exposed pads.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A researcher wants to test whether being underwater causes Limnophila's dissected leaves. What is the best design?
bank.a: Grow cuttings of the same plant, keep some shoots fully submerged and others in air, with the same light and temperature, and compare the shapes of the new leaves
d: Grow cuttings of the same plant, keep all shoots fully submerged under the same light and temperature, and record the new leaf shapes
Keep some shoots submerged in warm water and others in cool air, and compare the shapes of the new leaves
Collect leaves from plants in different ponds and on the banks, and compare their shapes
bank.why: Same genetics and conditions except submersion.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A student wants to test whether stipules protect young buds. Which design is best?
bank.a: Remove the stipules from some buds and leave others intact on the same plants, expose all to the same conditions, and compare bud damage
d: Remove the stipules from all the buds, expose them to the same conditions, and record how much bud damage occurs
Remove the stipules from some buds and leave others intact, but shade the intact buds only, and compare bud damage
Compare bud damage on a stipulate species with bud damage on an exstipulate species
bank.why: Same plants and conditions; only stipules differ.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.term: Experiment: leaf or branch by buds
bank.q: To decide whether a leafy axis is a compound leaf or a branch, what should be checked first?
bank.a: Whether buds are present in the axils of the leaflets and at the tip of the axis
d: How many leaflets it has and how they are arranged
How green the leaflets are compared with the leaves
How long the axis is compared with nearby branches
bank.why: Branches have axillary and terminal buds; compound leaves do not.

bank.term: Experiment: hairy leaves and water loss
bank.q: A researcher wants to test whether leaf hairs reduce water loss. What is the best design?
bank.a: Use leaves from the same plant, gently shave the hairs from some and leave others hairy, seal the cut ends, and weigh them at intervals in the same conditions
d: Use leaves from the same plant, shave the hairs from all of them, seal the cut ends, and weigh them at intervals
Shave some leaves and leave others hairy, but keep the shaved ones in the shade, and weigh them at intervals
Compare the weight loss of a hairy cactus pad with a smooth rose leaf in the same conditions
bank.why: Same species and conditions; only the hairs differ.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A researcher wants to test whether spines protect a plant from grazing. Which design is best?
bank.a: Remove spines from some plants and leave others intact in the same field with the same animals, then compare grazing damage over weeks
d: Remove the spines from all the plants in one field with the same animals, then record grazing damage over weeks
Remove spines from some plants in a grazed field and leave others intact in a fenced field, then compare damage
Remove the spines from one plant and leave another intact, and check them for grazing the next morning
bank.why: Same field and grazers; only spines differ.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A researcher wants to show that pitcher fluid digests insects. What is the best design?
bank.a: Place equal pieces of insect in pitcher fluid and in plain water (control) at the same temperature, and compare how much is broken down over a few days
d: Place equal pieces of insect in pitcher fluid at the same temperature, and record how much is broken down over a few days
Place insect pieces in pitcher fluid in the sun and in plain water in the shade, and compare how much breaks down
Place a large piece of insect in pitcher fluid and a small piece in plain water, and compare after a few days
bank.why: Only the liquid differs between the two containers.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: A student wants to test whether an Acacia's phyllodes photosynthesize. What is the best design?
bank.a: Cover some phyllodes with foil and leave others uncovered on the same plant, then test both for starch after a few days
d: Cover all the phyllodes with foil, then test them for starch after a few days
Cover some phyllodes on one Acacia and leave others uncovered on a different species, then test both for starch
Cover some phyllodes and leave others uncovered, then test only the uncovered ones for starch after a few days
bank.why: Only light reaching the phyllodes differs.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: Which part of the plant is the reproductive part, often its most beautiful and colorful part?
bank.why: The flower is the reproductive part of the plant.

dw.Leaf: The leaf makes food by photosynthesis.
dw.Stem: The stem supports the plant and carries materials.
dw.Root: The root anchors the plant and absorbs water.

bank.q: What is the biological function of a flower?
bank.a: To facilitate reproduction by providing a mechanism for the union of sperm with eggs
d: To store food reserves for the developing embryo inside the seed
To absorb water and minerals from the soil for the whole plant
To make food by photosynthesis for the rest of the shoot
bank.why: From the slides: it facilitates reproduction, usually by uniting sperm with eggs.

dw.To store food reserves for the developin: Storing food for the embryo is the job of the seed's endosperm or cotyledons.
dw.To absorb water and minerals from the so: Absorbing water and minerals is the job of the roots.
dw.To make food by photosynthesis for the r: Making food by photosynthesis is the job of the leaves.

bank.q: The world's smallest flower is...
bank.why: Wolffia is the smallest; Rafflesia is the largest.

dw.Datura: Datura is the slides' gamosepalous example.
dw.Brassica rapa: Brassica rapa is the slides' apetalous example.

bank.q: The world's largest flower is...
bank.why: Rafflesia is the largest flower.

dw.Datura: Datura is not the largest flower.
dw.Magnolia: Magnolia is not the largest flower; Rafflesia is.

bank.q: What are the four parts (whorls) of a flower?
bank.why: Calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.

dw.Sepal, petal, stamen, pedicel: Sepal, petal and stamen are units of whorls, and the pedicel is the flower stalk.
dw.Calyx, corolla, anther, ovule: Anther and ovule are parts inside whorls, not the four whorls.
dw.Stigma, style, ovary, filament: Stigma, style, ovary and filament are parts of the essential whorls.

bank.q: Which parts of the flower are classified as non-essential?
bank.why: Calyx and corolla are non-essential; androecium and gynoecium are essential.

bank.q: Which parts of the flower are classified as essential?
bank.why: The reproductive whorls are the essential parts.

dw.Calyx and corolla: Calyx and corolla are the non-essential whorls.
dw.Sepals and petals: Sepals and petals belong to the non-essential whorls.
dw.Corolla and androecium: The corolla is non-essential; only the androecium and gynoecium are essential.

bank.q: The outermost whorl of the flower, usually green and non-essential.
bank.why: Calyx: outermost whorl; its unit is the sepal.

dw.Corolla: The corolla is the second whorl.
dw.Androecium: The androecium is the third whorl.
dw.Gynoecium: The gynoecium is the innermost whorl.

bank.q: The separate unit of the calyx is called the...
bank.why: Calyx → sepals.

dw.Petal: The petal is the unit of the corolla.
dw.Stamen: The stamen is the unit of the androecium.
dw.Carpel: The carpel is the unit of the gynoecium.

bank.q: In some flowers the calyx is brightly colored. This is known as...
bank.why: A brightly colored calyx is petaloid (petal-like).

dw.Polysepalous: Polysepalous means free sepals, not their color.
dw.Apetalous: Apetalous means the petals are absent.

bank.q: What are the two types of calyx?
bank.why: Polysepalous: the sepals are free (rose). Gamosepalous: the sepals are fused (Datura). -sepalous = calyx; -petalous = corolla.

dw.Polypetalous and gamopetalous: Polypetalous and gamopetalous describe the corolla.
dw.Complete and incomplete: Complete and incomplete describe whole flowers.
dw.Staminate and pistillate: Staminate and pistillate describe unisexual flowers.

bank.q: Flowers whose sepals are free (separate) are called...
bank.why: Free sepals = polysepalous (e.g. rose). The slide's wording says 'petals', but it means sepals.

dw.Polypetalous: Polypetalous refers to free petals, not sepals.
dw.Petaloid: Petaloid means a brightly colored calyx.

bank.q: Flowers whose sepals are fused are called...
bank.why: Fused sepals = gamosepalous (e.g. Datura).

bank.q: Which flower is the slides' example of a polysepalous flower?
bank.why: Rose has free sepals.

dw.Brassica rapa: Brassica rapa is the apetalous example.
dw.Wolffia: Wolffia is the smallest flower, not a polysepalous example.

bank.q: Which flower is the slides' example of a gamosepalous flower?
bank.why: Datura has fused sepals.

dw.Brassica rapa: Brassica rapa is the apetalous example.
dw.Rafflesia: Rafflesia is the largest flower, not the gamosepalous example.

bank.q: The second whorl of the flower, non-essential and variously colored.
bank.why: Corolla: second whorl; units are petals.

dw.Calyx: The calyx is the first, outermost whorl.
dw.Androecium: The androecium is the third whorl.
dw.Gynoecium: The gynoecium is the innermost whorl.

bank.q: The individual part of the corolla is known as the...
bank.why: The corolla (2nd whorl) is made of petals. The calyx is made of sepals, the androecium of stamens, the gynoecium of carpels.

dw.Sepal: The sepal is the unit of the calyx.
dw.Stamen: The stamen is the unit of the androecium.
dw.Carpel: The carpel is the unit of the gynoecium.

bank.q: What are the three types of flowers based on the petals?
bank.why: By petals: polypetalous (free petals, rose), gamopetalous (fused petals, Datura) and apetalous (no petals, Brassica rapa).

dw.Polysepalous, gamosepalous, petaloid: Polysepalous, gamosepalous and petaloid describe the calyx.
dw.Complete, incomplete, bisexual: Complete, incomplete and bisexual describe whole flowers.
dw.Staminate, pistillate, bisexual: Staminate, pistillate and bisexual describe the sex of the flower.

bank.q: When the petals are free, the flower is called...
bank.why: Free petals: rose.

dw.Apetalous: Apetalous means the petals are absent.
dw.Polysepalous: Polysepalous describes the sepals, not the petals.

bank.q: Flowers with fused or united petals are called...
bank.why: United petals: Datura.

dw.Gamosepalous: Gamosepalous describes fused sepals, not petals.

bank.q: In some rare flowers the petals are absent. Such flowers are called...
bank.why: No petals: Brassica rapa.

dw.Petaloid: Petaloid is a brightly colored calyx.

bank.q: Which is the slides' example of an apetalous flower?
bank.why: Apetalous = petals absent, which is rare; the slides' example is Brassica rapa. Rose is polypetalous and Datura is gamopetalous.

bank.q: From the outside in, what is the order of the four whorls?
bank.why: 1st calyx, 2nd corolla, 3rd androecium, innermost gynoecium.

dw.Corolla → calyx → gynoecium → androecium: The calyx is the outermost whorl, not the corolla.
dw.Calyx → androecium → corolla → gynoecium: The corolla comes before the androecium.
dw.Gynoecium → androecium → corolla → calyx: That is the order from the inside out.

bank.q: A flower's outermost whorl is bright red and looks like petals, though its cells form sepals. What is this calyx called?
bank.why: A brightly colored calyx is petaloid.

dw.Gamosepalous: Gamosepalous describes fused sepals, not color.
dw.Apetalous: Apetalous means the petals are absent.

bank.term: Sepals pulled off one by one
bank.q: Each sepal of a flower can be pulled off separately without tearing the others. What type of calyx is this?
bank.why: Free sepals = polysepalous.

dw.Gamosepalous: Gamosepalous sepals are fused and cannot come off one by one.
dw.Gamopetalous: Gamopetalous describes fused petals, not sepals.

bank.term: Corolla comes off as one tube
bank.q: When a student pulls the corolla of a Datura flower, it comes off as a single tube. What type of corolla is this?
bank.why: Fused petals = gamopetalous.

dw.Polypetalous: Polypetalous petals come off one by one.
dw.Apetalous: Apetalous flowers have no corolla to pull.

bank.q: A mutant plant forms normal sepals, stamens and carpels, but its flowers are dull and attract few pollinators. Which whorl is most likely missing or reduced?
bank.why: The corolla is the variously colored whorl of petals.

bank.q: A flower bud keeps getting damaged before opening, though its petals, stamens and carpels develop normally. Which whorl, the outermost one, is most likely defective?
bank.why: The calyx is the outermost whorl.

bank.q: The third whorl of the flower: essential, male, its unit is the stamen.
bank.why: Androecium = male reproductive part.

dw.Gynoecium: The gynoecium is the female whorl.
dw.Corolla: The corolla is a non-essential whorl.
dw.Calyx: The calyx is a non-essential whorl.

bank.q: The separate unit of the androecium is known as the...
bank.why: The androecium (3rd whorl, male) is made of stamens; each stamen has an anther and a filament.

dw.Carpel: The carpel is the unit of the gynoecium.
dw.Petal: The petal is the unit of the corolla.
dw.Sepal: The sepal is the unit of the calyx.

bank.q: The powdery substance of the androecium responsible for pollination is called...
bank.why: Pollen grains in the anther are responsible for pollination.

dw.Ovules: Ovules are in the ovary and become seeds.
dw.Nectar: Nectar is a sugary reward for pollinators, not the powder.
dw.Endosperm: Endosperm is stored food in the seed.

bank.q: What are the two parts of the stamen?
bank.why: Anther (head, pollen) + filament (stalk).

dw.Stigma and style: Stigma and style are parts of the carpel.
dw.Ovary and ovule: Ovary and ovule are parts of the carpel.
dw.Sepal and petal: Sepal and petal are units of the calyx and corolla.

bank.q: The head part of the stamen, where the pollen grains are found.
bank.why: The anther is the head of the stamen and holds the pollen grains. The filament is the stalk that holds it up.

dw.Stigma: The stigma belongs to the carpel.
dw.Style: The style belongs to the carpel.

bank.q: The stalk that holds the anther.
bank.why: The filament is the stalk of the stamen that holds the anther. The style is the tube of the carpel.

dw.Style: The style is part of the carpel.
dw.Pedicel: The pedicel is the flower stalk.
dw.Stigma: The stigma is part of the carpel.

bank.q: The innermost whorl of the flower: essential, female, its unit is the carpel.
bank.why: Gynoecium = female part; after fertilization it develops into the fruit.

dw.Androecium: The androecium is the male whorl.

bank.q: The separate unit of the gynoecium is called the...
bank.why: The gynoecium (innermost whorl, female) is made of carpels: stigma, style and ovary.

dw.Stamen: The stamen is the unit of the androecium.
dw.Sepal: The sepal is the unit of the calyx.
dw.Petal: The petal is the unit of the corolla.

bank.q: After fertilization, the gynoecium develops into the...
bank.why: After fertilization the gynoecium (its ovary) develops into the fruit, and the ovules become the seeds.

dw.Seed: Seeds come from the ovules inside the gynoecium.
dw.Flower: The flower is the structure that carries the whorls.
dw.Leaf: The leaf is not formed from the flower.

bank.q: What are the three parts of the gynoecium (carpel)?
bank.why: A carpel has a stigma (sticky top), a style (the tube) and an ovary (with the ovules). Anther and filament belong to the stamen.

dw.Anther, filament, ovary: Anther and filament are parts of the stamen.
dw.Stigma, filament, ovule: The filament belongs to the stamen, and the ovule is inside the ovary.
dw.Style, anther, ovary: The anther is part of the stamen.

bank.q: The top part of the carpel, which is sticky so that pollen carried by pollinators sticks to it.
bank.why: The stigma is the sticky top of the carpel; pollen brought by pollinators sticks to it.

dw.Style: The style is the tube below the stigma.
dw.Ovary: The ovary is the base of the carpel.

bank.q: The tube in which the sperm cell enters and reaches the ovary.
bank.why: The style is the tube the sperm cell travels down to reach the ovary. The stigma is the sticky top.

dw.Stigma: The stigma is the sticky top.
dw.Filament: The filament holds up the anther.
dw.Ovule: The ovule is inside the ovary.

bank.q: The main part of the carpel where fertilization of sperm and eggs happens and which produces the eggs.
bank.why: The ovary has an ovary wall and ovules.

dw.Style: The style is the tube leading down.

bank.q: After fertilization, the ovary develops into the...
bank.why: Ovary → fruit; ovary wall → outer coat of the fruit; ovules → seeds.

dw.Seed: The ovules, not the ovary, become seeds.
dw.Seed coat: The seed coat comes from the ovule's covering.

bank.q: After fertilization, the ovary wall develops into the...
bank.why: Ovary → fruit, ovary wall → outer coat of the fruit, ovules → seeds.

dw.Seed coat of the seed: The seed coat covers the seed, not the fruit.
dw.Endosperm of the seed: The endosperm is stored food in the seed.
dw.Cotyledons of the embryo: Cotyledons belong to the embryo in the seed.

bank.q: After fertilization, the ovules develop into the...
bank.why: Ovules → seeds, while the ovary becomes the fruit and the ovary wall its outer coat.

dw.Fruit wall: The ovary wall becomes the fruit wall.
dw.Pollen grains: Pollen grains come from the anther.

bank.q: A flower that has all four whorls (calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium) is called...
bank.why: Most bisexual flowers are complete.

dw.Incomplete flower: An incomplete flower lacks a whorl.
dw.Unisexual flower: A unisexual flower has only one reproductive whorl.
dw.Pistillate flower: A pistillate flower is female, with no androecium.

bank.q: A flower in which any one of the four whorls is absent is called...
bank.why: All unisexual flowers are incomplete.

dw.Complete flower: A complete flower has all four whorls.
dw.Bisexual flower: Bisexual means both reproductive whorls are present.

bank.q: A flower in which both the androecium and gynoecium are present.
bank.why: Bisexual: androecium and gynoecium in the same flower. Unisexual flowers have only one: staminate (male) or pistillate (female).

dw.Unisexual flower: A unisexual flower has only one reproductive whorl.
dw.Staminate flower: A staminate flower has only the androecium.
dw.Pistillate flower: A pistillate flower has only the gynoecium.

bank.q: A male flower, with androecium present and gynoecium absent, is also known as...
bank.why: Male = staminate; female = pistillate.

bank.q: A female flower, with gynoecium present and androecium absent, is also known as...
bank.why: Female = pistillate (has the pistil).

bank.q: Which statement about unisexual flowers is correct?
bank.a: All unisexual flowers are incomplete flowers
d: All unisexual flowers are complete flowers
Unisexual flowers have both androecium and gynoecium
bank.why: A unisexual flower lacks one reproductive whorl, so it is incomplete.

dw.All unisexual flowers are complete flowe: Unisexual flowers are never complete; they are all incomplete.
dw.Unisexual flowers have both androecium a: Unisexual flowers have only one reproductive whorl.
dw.Unisexual flowers lack a calyx: Unisexual flowers may still have a calyx.

bank.q: According to the slides, most bisexual flowers are...
bank.why: Complete = all 4 whorls; most bisexual flowers are complete. All unisexual flowers are incomplete.

dw.Staminate flowers: Staminate flowers are male unisexual flowers.

bank.q: In the slides' figure, the stigma, style and ovary together are labeled the...
bank.why: The pistil is made of the carpel(s): stigma, style, ovary.

dw.Stamen: The stamen is the male unit.
dw.Pedicel: The pedicel is the flower stalk.
dw.Perianth: The perianth is the calyx and corolla together.

bank.q: Bees visit a flower and brush pollen onto its carpel, but the pollen never stays on it. Which part is most likely defective?
bank.why: The stigma is sticky so pollen sticks to it.

dw.Style: The style carries the sperm down; it does not catch pollen.
dw.Ovary: The ovary is where fertilization happens.

bank.q: Pollen sticks to a flower's stigma normally, but the sperm cell never reaches the ovary. Which part is most likely blocked?
bank.why: The style is the tube the sperm cell travels through to the ovary.

dw.Stigma: The pollen sticks, so the stigma works.
dw.Filament: The filament holds the anther up.

bank.q: After fertilization, a flower's ovary grows into a fruit with a normal outer coat, but no seeds form inside. What most likely failed to develop?
bank.why: Ovules develop into seeds.

dw.The ovary wall: The fruit has a normal outer coat, so the ovary wall formed.

bank.q: After fertilization, seeds develop normally but the fruit has no outer coat. Which part most likely failed to develop?
bank.why: The ovary wall becomes the outer coat of the fruit.

dw.The ovules: The seeds developed normally, so the ovules did.
dw.The style: The style only carries the sperm.
dw.The filament: The filament only holds up the anther.

bank.q: A flower has stamens with normal stalks, but no pollen is ever produced. Which part of the stamen is most likely defective?
bank.why: Pollen grains are found in the anther.

dw.Filament: The stalks are normal, so the filament works.
dw.Stigma: The stigma belongs to the carpel.
dw.Style: The style belongs to the carpel.

bank.q: A flower's anthers make pollen, but they lie limp at the base of the flower instead of being held up. Which part is most likely defective?
bank.why: The filament is the stalk that holds the anther.

dw.Style: The style belongs to the carpel.
dw.Stigma: The stigma belongs to the carpel.

bank.q: A flower has sepals, petals and stamens that release pollen, but it never forms a fruit, even when pollinated. What kind of flower is it most likely?
bank.why: With no gynoecium, there is nothing to develop into a fruit.

dw.A pistillate (female) flower: A pistillate flower would form fruit.
dw.A complete bisexual flower: A complete bisexual flower would also have a carpel and fruit.
dw.A petaloid flower: Petaloid describes only the calyx, not the sex.

bank.term: Fruits only if another flower's pollen arrives
bank.q: A flower has sepals, petals and a gynoecium but no stamens. It fruits only when pollen from another flower reaches it. Which describes this flower?
bank.why: A female flower lacks the androecium, so it is also incomplete.

dw.Staminate and complete: Staminate flowers have stamens, but this one has a gynoecium.
dw.Bisexual and complete: A bisexual complete flower would have stamens.
dw.Pistillate and complete: It is incomplete, since the stamens (a whorl) are missing.

bank.q: A flower has sepals, stamens and carpels but no petals. How is it classified?
d: Apetalous and complete, since it has stamens
Unisexual and incomplete, since it lacks petals
Polypetalous and complete, with both sexes
bank.why: Missing any whorl makes it incomplete; both reproductive whorls make it bisexual.

dw.Apetalous and complete, since it has sta: It has stamens and carpels, but missing petals make it incomplete, not complete.
dw.Unisexual and incomplete, since it lacks: It has both stamens and carpels, so it is not unisexual.
dw.Polypetalous and complete, with both sex: Polypetalous flowers have free petals; this one has none.

bank.q: A student wants to test whether pollinator visits are needed for a plant to set fruit. Which design is best?
bank.a: Bag some flowers to keep insects out and leave other flowers on the same plants unbagged, then compare how many set fruit
d: Bag all the flowers on one plant and leave all the flowers of a different plant unbagged, then count the fruits
Remove the petals from some flowers so insects cannot land, and compare fruit set with intact flowers
Count how many insects visit each plant for a week, then count the fruits on the plants that had the most visits
bank.why: Same plants and conditions; only pollinator access differs.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

dw.Bag all the flowers on one plant and lea: Comparing two different plants adds plant differences to the test.
dw.Remove the petals from some flowers so i: Removing petals changes the flower itself, not just insect access.
dw.Count how many insects visit each plant: This only observes a link; there is no control group.

bank.q: A researcher wants to test whether the stigma must be sticky to hold pollen. What is the best design?
bank.a: Gently wash the sticky coating off some stigmas and leave others untouched on the same plant, apply the same amount of pollen to both, then count the pollen that stays
d: Remove the whole carpel from some flowers and leave others intact, then compare how many fruits develop on each
Compare how much pollen sticks to the stigmas of two different plant species in the same garden
Wash the stigmas of every flower on the plant and count how much pollen sticks afterward
bank.why: Only the sticky coating differs; the pollen load is the same.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

dw.Remove the whole carpel from some flower: Removing the whole carpel tests more than stickiness.
dw.Compare how much pollen sticks to the st: Different species differ in many ways, not only stickiness.
dw.Wash the stigmas of every flower on the: With no untouched stigmas there is no control to compare.

bank.q: The structure known as a fruit is found only in the...
bank.why: Fruits are found only in angiosperms (flowering plants).

dw.Gymnosperms: Gymnosperms bear naked seeds, not fruits.

bank.q: A fruit developed solely from the ovary and its contents is known as a...
bank.why: True fruit: ovary only.

dw.Accessory fruit: An accessory fruit includes other flower parts.
dw.Multiple fruit: A multiple fruit comes from many flowers.
dw.Aggregate fruit: An aggregate fruit comes from many pistils of one flower.

bank.q: A fruit developed from the ovary and its contents plus other parts of the flower, such as the receptacle, petals and sepals, is called...
bank.why: Accessory fruit: e.g. pineapple; pomes are accessory too.

dw.True fruit: A true fruit comes from the ovary only.
dw.Simple fruit: Simple describes a fruit from one ovary, not the extra parts.
dw.Dry fruit: Dry describes the fruit wall, not its origin.

bank.q: Which is the slides' example of an accessory fruit?
bank.why: An accessory fruit forms from the ovary plus other parts (receptacle, petals, sepals); the slides' example is pineapple.

dw.Grape: Grape is a berry (a true fruit).
dw.Peach: Peach is a drupe (a true fruit).
dw.Bean: Bean is a legume (a true dry fruit).

bank.q: What are the three common classes of fruit types?
bank.why: Simple (one ovary), aggregate (many pistils of the same flower) and multiple (pistils of many flowers).

dw.Fleshy, dry, accessory: Fleshy, dry and accessory mix kinds of simple fruit with a different idea.
dw.Drupe, berry, pome: Drupe, berry and pome are fleshy fruit types.
dw.Dehiscent, indehiscent, capsule: Dehiscent, indehiscent and capsule are dry fruit types.

bank.q: A fruit that develops from a single ovary (one pistil) containing one or more carpels.
bank.why: Simple fruits may be true or accessory, fleshy or dry.

dw.Aggregate fruit: An aggregate fruit uses many pistils of one flower.
dw.Multiple fruit: A multiple fruit uses pistils of many flowers.
dw.Accessory fruit: Accessory describes extra flower parts, not the number of pistils.

bank.q: A fruit formed from a number of pistils of the same flower; its units may be berries or other types.
bank.why: Aggregate: many pistils, one flower.

dw.Multiple fruit: A multiple fruit uses pistils of many flowers.
dw.Simple fruit: A simple fruit comes from one pistil.
dw.Schizocarp: A schizocarp is a dry fruit that splits into mericarps.

bank.q: A fruit formed from a number of pistils, often with accessory parts, the pistils coming from a number of flowers (e.g. mulberry).
bank.why: Multiple: pistils from many flowers.

dw.Aggregate fruit: An aggregate fruit uses pistils of the same flower.
dw.Simple fruit: A simple fruit comes from one pistil.
dw.Pome: A pome comes from one flower.

bank.q: Which is the slides' example of a multiple fruit?
bank.why: A multiple fruit forms from the pistils of many flowers, often with accessory parts; the slides' example is mulberry.

bank.q: A simple fruit is either...
bank.why: A simple fruit comes from a single ovary and is either fleshy (drupe, berry, pome) or dry (dehiscent or indehiscent).

dw.Aggregate or multiple: Aggregate and multiple are separate fruit classes.
dw.True or accessory only: True and accessory describe origin, not the two simple types.
dw.Drupe or legume only: Drupe and legume are single types, not the two categories.

bank.q: A fruit in which the wall becomes soft and fleshy as it matures.
bank.why: Fleshy fruit: the wall becomes soft at maturity (drupe, berry, pome). In a dry fruit the coat becomes dry.

dw.Dry fruit: A dry fruit's wall becomes dry.
dw.Dehiscent fruit: Dehiscent fruits are dry fruits that open.
dw.Capsule: A capsule is a dry dehiscent fruit.

bank.q: What are the three types of fleshy fruits?
bank.why: The three fleshy fruits are the drupe (stony pit), berry (juicy ovary wall) and pome (apple, accessory).

dw.Legume, follicle, capsule: Legume, follicle and capsule are dry dehiscent fruits.
dw.Achene, nut, samara: Achene, nut and samara are dry indehiscent fruits.
dw.Hesperidium, pepo, legume: The legume is a dry fruit; hesperidium and pepo are special berries.

bank.q: A one-seeded simple fruit from a superior ovary whose innermost wall becomes hard and stony.
bank.why: Drupe: thin exocarp, fleshy or fibrous mesocarp, stony endocarp (cherry, peach, plum).

dw.Berry: A berry has no stony pit.
dw.Pome: A pome is an accessory fruit.
dw.Nut: A nut is a dry fruit.

bank.q: In a drupe, which layer becomes hard and stony?
bank.why: Endocarp = innermost layer = the stone/pit.

dw.Exocarp: The exocarp is the thin skin.
dw.Mesocarp: The mesocarp is the fleshy or fibrous middle.
dw.Seed coat: The seed coat belongs to the seed, not the fruit wall.

bank.q: In a drupe, the outermost part that becomes a relatively thin skin is the...
bank.why: Drupe: exocarp = thin skin (outer), mesocarp = fleshy or fibrous middle, endocarp = hard, stony pit (inner).

dw.Endocarp: The endocarp is the stony pit.
dw.Mesocarp: The mesocarp is the middle layer.
dw.Pericarp core: The pericarp is the whole fruit wall, not the skin.

bank.q: In a drupe, the middle portion between the skin and the stone, which becomes fleshy or fibrous, is the...
bank.why: The mesocarp is the middle layer, the flesh. The exocarp is the skin and the endocarp is the stony pit.

dw.Exocarp: The exocarp is the thin skin.
dw.Endocarp: The endocarp is the stony pit.

bank.q: In a drupe, the hard stony pit comes from which layer of the ovary?
bank.a: The inner tissue layer of the ovary
d: The outer tissue layer of the ovary
The middle layer of the ovary
bank.why: Skin = outer layer, flesh = middle layer, pit = inner layer.

dw.The outer tissue layer of the ovary: The outer layer becomes the thin skin.
dw.The middle layer of the ovary: The middle layer becomes the flesh.
dw.The receptacle: The receptacle is not part of the ovary.

bank.q: Which set lists drupes from the slides?
bank.why: Drupes: cherry, peach, plum and coconut (a drupe with fibrous walls). Grape and banana are berries; apple and pear are pomes.

bank.q: How is the coconut different from most drupes?
bank.a: It has fibrous walls instead of fleshy walls
d: It has many seeds instead of a single seed in the pit
It splits open at maturity to release its seed
It forms from the pistils of several flowers
bank.why: The coconut husk is fibrous; inside are liquid and solid endosperm.

dw.It has many seeds instead of a single se: A coconut drupe has one seed.
dw.It splits open at maturity to release it: A coconut does not split open.
dw.It forms from the pistils of several flo: A coconut forms from one flower, not many.

bank.q: In a coconut, the coconut water and the white meat are the...
bank.why: The slide labels liquid endosperm and solid endosperm.

dw.Pericarp: The pericarp is the fruit wall, not the water and meat.

bank.q: A simple fruit in which the ovary wall, or at least its inner portions, becomes enlarged and usually juicy (grape, banana, gooseberry).
bank.why: Berry: the ovary wall (at least its inner part) becomes enlarged and juicy: grape, banana, gooseberry, tomato.

dw.Drupe: A drupe has a stony pit.
dw.Pome: A pome is an accessory fruit.
dw.Achene: An achene is a dry fruit.

bank.q: Which set lists berries from the slides?
bank.why: Berries: grape, banana, gooseberry, tomato. Cherry, peach and plum are drupes; apple and pear are pomes.

bank.q: What are the two special types of berries?
bank.why: Hesperidium (leathery rind: orange, lemon) and pepo (hard rind: watermelon, squash, cucumber).

dw.Drupe and pome: Drupe and pome are separate fleshy fruit types.
dw.Legume and follicle: Legume and follicle are dry fruits.

bank.q: A special berry with a leathery rind, its interior divided by septa that show the number of carpels.
bank.why: Citrus: orange, lemon.

dw.Pepo: A pepo has a hard rind, not a leathery rind with septa.
dw.Pome: A pome is an accessory fruit.
dw.Drupe: A drupe has a stony pit.

bank.q: In a hesperidium, the septa dividing the interior indicate the number of...
bank.why: In a hesperidium (orange, lemon) the septa that divide the inside show the number of carpels.

dw.Seeds: The septa show the carpels, not the seeds.
dw.Flowers: A fruit forms from one flower.

bank.q: A berry with a relatively hard rind (watermelon, gourds, squash).
bank.why: Also pumpkin and cucumber.

dw.Hesperidium: A hesperidium has a leathery rind and septa.
dw.Pome: A pome is an accessory fruit.
dw.Drupe: A drupe has a stony pit.

bank.q: The word pome comes from the French name for...
bank.why: Pome comes from the French pomme, apple. Apple, pear and mountain ash are pomes.

dw.A pear: Pomme is the French word for apple.
dw.A fruit: Pomme names one fruit, the apple.

bank.q: An accessory fleshy fruit formed by a group of carpels united with each other and surrounded by the floral tube or receptacle (apple, pear).
bank.why: Tissue comes from both the ovary and the perianth.

dw.Drupe: A drupe is a true fruit with a stony pit.
dw.Berry: A berry is a true fruit.
dw.Hesperidium: A hesperidium is a berry with a leathery rind.

bank.q: Why is a pome often called an accessory fruit?
bank.a: Its tissue comes from both the ovary and the perianth
d: It forms from the pistils of several different flowers
It has a single seed inside a hard stony pit
It splits open along its seams when it is ripe
bank.why: In a pome the core comes from the ovary and the pulp from the perianth (floral tube), so it is an accessory fruit.

dw.It splits open along its seams when it i: That describes a dehiscent dry fruit.

bank.q: In an apple, the core comes from the ___ and the pulp comes from the ___.
bank.why: The slide labels: core (from ovary), pulp (from perianth).

dw.Receptacle; seeds: The receptacle is the flower base, and the seeds are not the pulp.
dw.Endocarp; seed coat: The endocarp and seed coat are not the core and pulp of a pome.

bank.q: A pome is composed of how many carpels?
bank.why: Five or more carpels; the exocarp is an inconspicuous layer.

dw.One: One carpel is far too few for a pome.

bank.q: Which set lists pomes from the slides?
bank.why: Pomes: apple, pear, mountain ash. Cherry and plum are drupes; orange and lemon are hesperidia; watermelon and squash are pepos.

bank.q: A fleshy, one-seeded fruit has a thin skin and a hard stony pit that cracks open to reveal a single seed. What type of fruit is it?

dw.Berry: A berry has no stony pit.
dw.Pome: A pome has a core, not a stony pit.
dw.Pepo: A pepo has a hard rind and many seeds.

bank.q: A juicy fruit has a leathery rind, and its inside is divided by thin partitions into segments. What type of fruit is it?
bank.why: Leathery rind + septa = hesperidium (citrus).

dw.Pepo: A pepo has a hard rind without partitions.
dw.Drupe: A drupe has a stony pit.

bank.q: A large fleshy fruit has a hard rind and many seeds in its juicy interior, like a squash. What type of fruit is it?
bank.why: A berry with a relatively hard rind is a pepo.

dw.Hesperidium: A hesperidium has a leathery rind with septa.
dw.Drupe: A drupe has one seed in a stony pit.

bank.term: Edible part not from the ovary
bank.q: In a fleshy fruit, the edible pulp comes from the perianth, while the seeds sit in a core formed by the ovary. What type of fruit is it?
bank.why: Pome = accessory fruit: core from ovary, pulp from perianth.

dw.Berry: A berry's pulp comes from the ovary wall.
dw.Drupe: A drupe has a stony pit.
dw.Hesperidium: A hesperidium has a leathery rind.

bank.q: A fruit forms from one flower that had many separate pistils, each becoming a small unit of the fruit. What kind of fruit is it?
bank.why: Many pistils of the same flower = aggregate.

dw.Multiple fruit: A multiple fruit comes from several flowers.
dw.Simple fruit: A simple fruit comes from one pistil.
dw.Schizocarp: A schizocarp is a dry fruit.

bank.q: A single fruit forms from the pistils of many flowers in a cluster, like a mulberry. What kind of fruit is it?
bank.why: Pistils from a number of flowers = multiple fruit.

dw.Aggregate fruit: An aggregate fruit comes from one flower.
dw.Simple fruit: A simple fruit comes from one pistil.
dw.Berry: A berry is one fleshy simple fruit.

bank.q: A one-seeded fruit has a hard stony layer around the seed, but the layer outside it is a thick fibrous husk instead of soft flesh. What is it?
bank.why: Coconuts are drupes with fibrous walls.

dw.A pome, like the apple: A pome has a core and is an accessory fruit.
dw.A berry, like the grape: A berry has no stony pit.
dw.A nut, like the acorn: A nut is dry; the coconut is a fibrous, fleshy-type drupe.

bank.q: A student wants to check whether the number of segments in citrus fruits matches the number of carpels in their flowers. Which approach is best?

Count the segments of an orange and a lemon and check whether the two numbers are the same
Count the seeds inside several fruits and take that as the number of carpels in each flower
