dw.Count the seeds inside several fruits an: The number of seeds does not equal the number of carpels.

bank.q: A fruit in which the coat becomes dry at maturity.
bank.why: Dry fruit: the coat is dry at maturity; it is either dehiscent (opens) or indehiscent (stays closed).

dw.Fleshy fruit: A fleshy fruit has a soft wall.

bank.q: What are the two major types of dry fruits?
bank.why: Dehiscent fruits open along definite seams; indehiscent fruits do not open and are often one-seeded.

dw.Fleshy and dry: Fleshy and dry are the two simple fruit categories.
dw.Simple and aggregate: Simple and aggregate are fruit classes.
dw.Loculicidal and septicidal: Loculicidal and septicidal are capsule types.

bank.q: Dry fruits that, at maturity, open by definite natural seams to shed the contained seeds.
bank.why: Dehiscent = opens along definite seams to shed the seeds (legume, follicle, capsule).

dw.Accessory fruits: Accessory describes the origin of the fruit.

bank.q: Dry fruits that do not open when mature to shed their seeds; many are one-seeded.
bank.why: Indehiscent = does not open at maturity; many are one-seeded (achene, nut, samara, grain, schizocarp).

bank.q: Which are the types of dehiscent fruits in the slides?
bank.why: Dehiscent: legume, follicle and capsule. Achene, nut and samara are indehiscent; drupe, berry and pome are fleshy.

bank.q: A dry dehiscent fruit from one carpel that, at maturity, splits along both the dorsal and ventral sutures (beans, peas).
bank.why: Two seams.

dw.Follicle: A follicle splits along only one suture.
dw.Silique: A silique is a capsule of two carpels.

bank.q: A legume develops from a simple ovary (one carpel) with...
bank.why: A legume comes from one carpel with two rows of ovules, and splits along both sutures (pea, bean).

dw.One ovule: A legume has two rows of ovules.
dw.No ovules: A legume has ovules, in two rows.

bank.q: Which legume is one of the few that does not split open when ripe?
bank.why: Probably because the peanut develops in the soil rather than in the air.

dw.Larkspur: Larkspur makes a follicle, not a legume.

bank.q: Why does the peanut probably not split open when ripe?
bank.a: Its fruit develops in the soil rather than in the air
d: Its pod comes from several carpels joined together
Its pod has no seeds inside when it ripens
Its pod wall stays soft and fleshy instead of drying
bank.why: The peanut is one of the few legumes that don't split, probably because its fruit develops in the soil.

dw.Its pod comes from several carpels joine: A peanut pod has one carpel.

bank.q: A dry dehiscent fruit from one carpel that splits along only one suture (larkspur, columbine).
bank.why: One seam, always lengthwise along one edge of the carpel.

dw.Legume: A legume splits along both sutures.

bank.q: Which plants produce follicles according to the slides?
bank.why: Also bay magnolia (Magnolia virginiana).

bank.q: What is the key difference between a legume and a follicle?
bank.a: A legume splits along two edges of the carpel; a follicle along one
d: A legume has several carpels; a follicle develops from only one
A follicle does not split at all; a legume splits along one edge
A legume is a fleshy fruit; a follicle is a dry fruit
bank.why: Both come from one carpel: a legume splits along two sutures (dorsal and ventral), a follicle along one.

dw.A legume has several carpels; a follicle: Both legume and follicle come from one carpel.
dw.A follicle does not split at all; a legu: A follicle does split along one edge.

bank.q: A dry dehiscent fruit developed from several carpels.
bank.why: Unlike the legume, it has more than one carpel.

bank.q: Unlike the legume, the capsule is composed of...
bank.why: A capsule has several carpels; a legume and a follicle each come from one carpel.

dw.Only one carpel: A legume has only one carpel.
dw.A fleshy wall: A capsule is a dry fruit.

bank.q: Fruits like the lily split lengthwise into sections corresponding to the number of...
bank.why: A capsule like the lily splits lengthwise into as many sections as it has carpels.

dw.Seeds: The sections match the carpels, not the seeds.
dw.Petals: Petals are not part of the fruit wall.
dw.Stamens: Stamens are not part of the gynoecium.

bank.q: A capsule that splits along the outer median line (lilies).
bank.why: Examples: lily, Viola, Yucca, Datura.

dw.Septicidal capsule: Septicidal capsules split along the septa.
dw.Denticidal capsule: Denticidal capsules open by small teeth.

bank.q: A capsule that opens with round holes (poppies).
bank.why: Papaver: seeds escape through pores.

dw.Loculicidal capsule: Loculicidal capsules split along the median line.
dw.Pyxis: A pyxis opens like a lid.

bank.q: A capsule in which small teeth at the top split open to release the seeds, as in corn cockle.
bank.why: Agrostemma githago.

dw.Poricidal capsule: Poricidal capsules open by round holes.
dw.Septicidal capsule: Septicidal capsules split along the septa.
dw.Silicle: A silicle is a short, broad capsule.

bank.q: A capsule that splits along the septa and opens at the top (Dutchman's pipe).
bank.why: Aristolochia.

dw.Loculicidal capsule: Loculicidal capsules split along the outer median line.
dw.Poricidal capsule: Poricidal capsules open by round holes.

bank.q: A special long, slender capsule of two carpels, typical of the mustard family.
bank.why: Brassicaceae (Cruciferae).

dw.Silicle: A silicle is short and broad.

bank.q: A special short, broad capsule of two carpels.
bank.why: Silicle = short and broad, 2 carpels. Silique = long and slender, 2 carpels (mustard family).

dw.Silique: A silique is long and slender.
dw.Pyxis: A pyxis opens like a lid.
dw.Samara: A samara is an indehiscent winged fruit.

bank.q: A capsule with circumscissile dehiscence, opening like a lid (plantain).
bank.why: Pyxis: circumscissile dehiscence, the top comes off like a lid (plantain).

dw.Silicle: A silicle is a short, broad capsule.
dw.Poricidal capsule: A poricidal capsule opens by holes.
dw.Septicidal capsule: A septicidal capsule splits along the septa.

bank.q: The typical fruit of the mustard family (Brassicaceae or Cruciferae) is the...
bank.why: The silique (long, slender, 2 carpels) is the typical fruit of the mustard family, Brassicaceae or Cruciferae.

dw.Legume: A legume is the pea family's fruit.
dw.Pome: A pome is a fleshy fruit.
dw.Achene: An achene is a one-seeded dry fruit.

bank.q: In siliques and silicles, the partition (septum) that bears the seeds after the valves fall is labeled the...
bank.why: The figures label valves and the replum.

dw.Locule: A locule is a seed chamber.
dw.Pedicel: The pedicel is the flower stalk.
dw.Mericarp: A mericarp is a piece of a schizocarp.

bank.q: Match: poppy (Papaver) has which type of capsule?
bank.why: Poricidal capsules open by round holes (poppy, Papaver).

dw.Loculicidal: Loculicidal capsules split along the median line.
dw.Septicidal: Septicidal capsules split along the septa.

bank.q: Corn cockle (Agrostemma githago) has which type of capsule?
bank.why: Denticidal capsules open by small teeth at the top (corn cockle, Agrostemma githago).

dw.Loculicidal: Loculicidal capsules split along the median line (lily).
dw.Septicidal: Septicidal capsules split along the septa.

bank.q: Dutchman's pipe (Aristolochia) has which type of capsule?
bank.why: Septicidal capsules split along the septa and open at the top (Dutchman's pipe, Aristolochia).

bank.q: Lilies, Viola and Yucca have which type of capsule?
bank.why: Loculicidal capsules split along the outer median line (lily, Viola, Yucca, Datura).

bank.q: Which are the types of indehiscent fruits in the slides?
bank.why: Indehiscent: achene, nut, samara, grain (caryopsis) and schizocarp. Legume, follicle and capsule are dehiscent.

bank.q: A one-seeded, dry, indehiscent fruit whose seed is attached to the fruit wall at a single point (buttercup, dandelion, sunflower).
bank.why: The seed is free of the pericarp except at one point.

dw.Nut: A nut has a hard, thick wall.
dw.Grain: A grain has a seed coat fused to the wall.

bank.q: In the slides, the fruit wall is also called the...
bank.why: The fruit wall is the pericarp (from the ovary wall). The testa is the seed coat; the involucre forms the acorn cup.

dw.Endosperm: Endosperm is stored food in the seed.
dw.Testa: The testa is the seed coat.
dw.Involucre: The involucre forms the acorn cup.

bank.q: Which set lists achenes from the slides?
bank.why: Achenes: buttercup, dandelion, sunflower. Oak, chestnut and hazel are nuts; elm, maple and ash are samaras.

bank.q: A dry, indehiscent, one-seeded fruit similar to an achene but with the wall greatly thickened and hardened.
bank.why: Beech, chestnut, oak (acorn), hazel.

dw.Achene: An achene has a thin wall.

bank.q: Why are walnut and hickory sometimes called drupes?
bank.a: Because of their extrafloral bracts, or husk
d: Because they split open when ripe
Because they form from several flowers
bank.why: Walnut and hickory are nuts, but their husk (extrafloral bracts) makes them look like drupes.

bank.q: In an acorn, the cup is derived from the...
bank.why: The acorn cup comes from the involucre (bracts), not from the ovary wall.

dw.Ovary wall: The ovary wall is the fruit wall.
dw.Seed coat: The seed coat covers the seed.
dw.Receptacle: The cup comes from the involucre, not the receptacle.

bank.q: A one- or two-seeded dry, indehiscent fruit in which part of the fruit wall grows out into a wing (elm, maple, ash).
bank.why: An achene with a wing for wind dispersal.

dw.Nut: A nut has a hard, thick wall.

bank.q: The samara is described as an achene with a wing for...
bank.why: A samara is a winged achene (elm, maple, ash); the wing carries it on the wind.

dw.Water dispersal: The wing helps the wind, not water, carry it.
dw.Animal dispersal: The wing is for wind, not for animals.
dw.Explosive dispersal: The wing is not for explosive dispersal.

bank.q: A one-seeded fruit whose seed coat is fused to the pericarp.
bank.why: Wheat, corn.

dw.Achene: In an achene the seed is free of the wall.
dw.Nut: A nut has a thick, hard wall.

bank.q: What separates an achene from a grain (caryopsis)?
bank.a: In a grain the seed coat is fused to the fruit wall; in an achene the seed is free except at one point
d: An achene grows a wing for wind dispersal; a grain never has a wing
A grain splits open at maturity; an achene stays closed
An achene holds many seeds; a grain holds only one seed
bank.why: Grain (caryopsis): the seed coat is fused to the pericarp (wheat, corn). Achene: the seed is free, attached at one point.

dw.An achene grows a wing for wind dispersa: The wing belongs to the samara, not the achene or grain.
dw.A grain splits open at maturity; an ache: Neither splits open; both are indehiscent.
dw.An achene holds many seeds; a grain hold: An achene holds one seed, like a grain.

bank.q: A fruit from a compound pistil that splits into mericarps, pieces that enclose one or more seeds and resemble fruits themselves.
bank.why: A schizocarp comes from a compound pistil and splits into mericarps that look like small fruits.

dw.Aggregate fruit: An aggregate fruit is fleshy and made from many pistils.

bank.q: The pieces into which a schizocarp splits are called...
bank.why: A schizocarp splits into mericarps, each holding one or more seeds.

dw.Carpels: Carpels are the parts of the pistil.
dw.Valves: Valves are the pieces a capsule splits into.

bank.q: A dry pod from a single carpel splits open along both its upper and lower seams when ripe. What type of fruit is it?
bank.why: Both sutures = legume.

dw.Follicle: A follicle splits along one edge.

bank.q: A dry fruit from a single carpel opens along only one edge to release its seeds. What type of fruit is it?
bank.why: One suture = follicle.

dw.Legume: A legume splits along both edges.

bank.q: A legume plant forms normal pods, but the pods never split open. Unlike other legumes, the pods ripen underground. Which plant is it most likely?
bank.why: The peanut develops in the soil and does not split.

bank.q: A dry capsule releases its seeds only through small round holes near its top when shaken by the wind. What type of capsule is it?
bank.why: Opening by pores = poricidal (poppy).

dw.Pyxis: A pyxis opens like a lid.

bank.term: Top comes off like a lid
bank.q: A capsule opens when its upper part comes off like a lid, cut all around. What type is it?
bank.why: Circumscissile dehiscence = pyxis.

dw.Silicle: A silicle splits into two valves.
dw.Septicidal capsule: A septicidal capsule splits along the septa.
dw.Denticidal capsule: A denticidal capsule opens by teeth.

bank.q: A dry, one-seeded fruit spins away from the tree because part of its wall grows into a flat wing. What type of fruit is it?
bank.why: Winged indehiscent fruit = samara.

dw.Nut: A nut has a thick, hard wall.

bank.term: Can't separate seed from fruit wall
bank.q: A student tries to peel the fruit wall from a corn kernel but finds the seed coat completely fused to it. What type of fruit is a corn kernel?
bank.why: Seed coat fused to the pericarp = grain.

dw.Achene: In an achene the seed is free of the wall.
dw.Nut: A nut has a thick, hard wall.
dw.Legume: A legume is a pod from one carpel.

bank.term: Seed loose inside a thin wall
bank.q: A dry one-seeded fruit like a sunflower 'seed' has a thin wall, and the seed inside is attached at only one point. What type of fruit is it?
bank.why: Achene: seed free of the pericarp except at a single point.

dw.Grain: In a grain the seed coat is fused to the wall.
dw.Nut: A nut has a hard, thick wall.

bank.q: A dry, one-seeded fruit like an acorn does not open, and its wall is greatly thickened and hard. What type of fruit is it?
bank.why: A nut is like an achene with a very hard wall.

dw.Achene: An achene has a thin wall.
dw.Grain: A grain has a seed coat fused to the wall.

bank.q: A dry fruit from a compound pistil breaks into two pieces when ripe, and each piece holds a seed and looks like a small fruit. What type is it?
bank.why: Pieces = mericarps; the whole fruit is a schizocarp.

dw.Legume: A legume splits along its seams.

bank.q: A researcher wants to test whether peanut pods stay closed because they ripen in the soil. Which design is best?
bank.a: On the same plants, let some pods ripen buried in soil and hold others up in the air in mesh bags, then compare how many split open
d: Compare whether peanut pods and pea pods split open when both are left to ripen in the same field
Bury all the pods of one peanut plant and keep all the pods of another plant in the air, then compare
Count the seeds in each peanut pod, since pods with more seeds should be more likely to split open
bank.why: Same plants; only where the pods ripen differs.

dw.Compare whether peanut pods and pea pods: Pea and peanut differ in many ways.
dw.Bury all the pods of one peanut plant an: Using different plants adds plant differences; pods of the same plant give a better test.
dw.Count the seeds in each peanut pod, sinc: Seed count is not the factor being tested.

bank.q: A student wants to test whether a maple samara's wing helps it travel farther. What is the best design?
bank.a: Trim the wings off some samaras and leave others intact, drop all from the same height in the same breeze, and measure how far each lands
d: Drop one winged samara from a balcony on a windy day and measure how far away from the building it lands
Drop maple samaras and acorns from the same height in the same breeze and compare their distances
Drop winged samaras from different heights in the same breeze and compare how far each one travels
bank.why: Only the wing differs; height and wind are the same.

dw.Drop one winged samara from a balcony on: One samara once is not a replicated test.
dw.Drop maple samaras and acorns from the s: Samara versus acorn changes more than the wing.
dw.Drop winged samaras from different heigh: Different heights test height, not the wing.

bank.q: A fertilized matured ovule together covered with a seed coat, which serves as a propagating material.
bank.why: A seed is an embryonic plant enclosed in a protective outer covering.

dw.Fruit: The fruit is the ripened ovary.
dw.Embryo: The embryo is only one part of the seed.

bank.q: According to the slides, the formation of the seed...
bank.a: Completes the process of reproduction in seed plants
d: Starts the process of pollination in flowering plants
Happens before fertilization of the egg in the ovary
Occurs only in gymnosperms, never in flowering plants
bank.why: The seed, a fertilized matured ovule with a seed coat, completes reproduction in seed plants.

dw.Starts the process of pollination in flo: Pollination comes before the seed forms.
dw.Happens before fertilization of the egg: Seeds form after fertilization, not before.
dw.Occurs only in gymnosperms, never in flo: Seeds form in flowering plants too.

bank.q: What are the three basic parts of a typical seed?
bank.why: A seed has an embryo, endosperm (stored food) and a seed coat (testa).

dw.Ovary, ovule, style: Ovary, ovule and style are flower parts.
dw.Cotyledon, radicle, pericarp: Cotyledon and radicle are embryo parts, and the pericarp is the fruit wall.
dw.Anther, filament, pollen: Anther, filament and pollen belong to the stamen.

bank.q: In the 'Parts of a seed' figure, the stored food is the...
bank.why: The endosperm is the stored food of the seed; the embryo is the young plant and the testa the seed coat.

dw.Embryo: The embryo is the young plant.
dw.Seed coat: The seed coat is the outer covering.
dw.Micropyle: The micropyle is a small opening in the seed coat.

bank.q: In the seed diagram, the outer covering labeled testa is the...
bank.why: The testa is the seed coat, the protective outer covering.

dw.Cotyledon: The cotyledon is part of the embryo.
dw.Radicle: The radicle is the embryonic root.

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the characteristics of a good seed in the slides?
bank.a: It must be as large as possible
d: It must be true to its type
It must be viable, with tested germination capacity
It must not be affected by any seed-borne disease
bank.why: A good seed is true to type, healthy and pure, viable, uniform and free from seed-borne disease. Size is not on the list.

dw.It must be true to its type: Being true to type is a characteristic of a good seed.
dw.It must be viable, with tested germinati: Viability is a characteristic of a good seed.
dw.It must not be affected by any seed-born: Freedom from seed-borne disease is a characteristic.

bank.q: A good seed must be healthy, pure and free from...
bank.why: Pure means free from inert materials and weed seeds.

dw.Endosperm and stored food: Endosperm is part of a good seed.
dw.Cotyledons and embryo axis: The embryo is part of a good seed.
dw.Its natural seed coat: The seed coat is part of a good seed.

bank.q: A good seed must be viable, meaning its germination capacity is...
bank.a: Up to the standard and has been tested recently
d: Unknown until the seeds are planted in the field
Kept below 10 percent so the seeds store longer
Not important as long as the seeds look healthy

dw.Kept below 10 percent so the seeds store: Germination capacity should be up to the standard, not below.

bank.q: Seeds with only one cotyledon (wheat, corn, rice) are called...
bank.why: Monocots have 1 cotyledon (wheat, corn, rice); dicots have 2 (pea, bean, mango).

dw.Recalcitrant seeds: Recalcitrant seeds are stored badly after drying.

bank.q: Seeds with two cotyledons (pea, bean, mango) are called...
bank.why: Dicots have 2 cotyledons (pea, bean, mango); monocots have 1 (wheat, corn, rice).

bank.q: Germination in monocot seeds is usually...
bank.why: Hypogeal: cotyledon stays below ground.

dw.Epigeal (except in pea and gram): Epigeal germination is typical of most dicots.
dw.Viviparous: Vivipary is germination on the parent plant.

bank.q: Germination in dicot seeds is usually...
bank.why: Epigeal: cotyledons come above ground.

dw.Hypogeal (except in onion): Hypogeal germination is typical of most monocots.

bank.q: Which monocot is the exception that does NOT have hypogeal germination?
bank.why: Monocots usually have hypogeal germination (cotyledon stays below ground), except onion.

bank.q: Which dicots are the exceptions that do NOT have epigeal germination?
bank.why: Dicots usually have epigeal germination (cotyledons come above ground), except pea and gram.

dw.Castor and poppy: Castor and poppy are albuminous seeds.
dw.Coffee and neem: Coffee and neem are recalcitrant seeds.

bank.q: Which set of features belongs to monocot seeds/plants in the slides?
bank.a: Adventitious roots, no secondary growth, usually endospermic
d: Secondary growth often present, usually non-endospermic
Flower parts in fours or fives, epigeal germination
bank.why: Monocots: 1 cotyledon, adventitious roots, no secondary growth, usually endospermic, hypogeal germination (except onion).

dw.Flower parts in fours or fives, epigeal: Flower parts in fours or fives and epigeal germination are dicot features.
dw.Two cotyledons, tap root: Two cotyledons and a tap root are dicot features.

bank.q: Which set of features belongs to dicot seeds/plants in the slides?
bank.a: Usually non-endospermic, secondary growth often present, flower parts in multiples of four or five
d: Usually endospermic, no secondary growth, flower parts in multiples of three
One cotyledon, adventitious roots, hypogeal germination except onion
Two cotyledons, usually endospermic, hypogeal germination except pea and gram
bank.why: Dicots: 2 cotyledons, usually non-endospermic, secondary growth often present, flower parts in 4s or 5s, epigeal (except pea and gram).

dw.Two cotyledons, usually endospermic, hyp: That set includes a feature that is not a dicot trait.

bank.q: Seeds with endosperm (castor, poppy, custard apple) are called...
bank.why: Albuminous (endospermic) seeds keep their endosperm: castor, poppy, custard apple. Exalbuminous seeds have none: gram, pea, bean.

bank.q: Seeds without endosperm (gram, pea, bean) are called...
bank.why: Their food is stored in the cotyledons.

bank.q: Which set lists albuminous seeds from the slides?
bank.why: Albuminous: castor, poppy, custard apple. Gram, pea and bean are exalbuminous; coffee, mango and rubber are recalcitrant.

bank.q: Seeds that survive drying and/or freezing during ex-situ conservation and can be stored for a longer period.

dw.10 to 20 percent: 10 to 20% is too dry for a recalcitrant seed.

bank.q: Which set lists recalcitrant seeds from the slides?
bank.why: Recalcitrant: coffee, mango, rubber, neem, jackfruit. They die when dried and are sensitive to chilling.

dw.Rice, wheat, maize: Those are grains, which are orthodox.

bank.q: Which set lists orthodox seeds from the slides?
bank.a: Capsicum annuum, Citrus aurantifolia, most grains and legumes
bank.why: Orthodox: Capsicum annuum, Citrus aurantifolia, most grains and legumes. They survive drying and freezing.

dw.Neem, jackfruit, Capsicum annuum, coffee: Neem, jackfruit and coffee are recalcitrant.
dw.Rubber, mango, Citrus aurantifolia, coff: Rubber, mango and coffee are recalcitrant.

bank.q: Based on the food we get from seeds, rice, wheat, jowar, maize and ragi are...
bank.why: By food: grains (rice, wheat, jowar, maize, ragi), pulses (grams, peas, beans), oilseeds (groundnut, sesame, mustard, coconut, sunflower).

dw.Pulses: Pulses are grams, peas and beans.
dw.Legumes only: Rice and wheat are not legumes.

bank.q: Based on the food we get from seeds, grams, peas and beans are...
bank.why: Pulses: grams, peas and beans. Rice and wheat are grains; groundnut and sesame are oilseeds.

dw.Grains: Grains are rice, wheat, jowar, maize and ragi.
dw.Cereals: Cereals are grains such as rice and wheat.

bank.q: Based on the food we get from seeds, groundnut, sesame, mustard, coconut and sunflower seed are...
bank.why: Oilseeds: groundnut, sesame, mustard, coconut, sunflower. Grains are rice, wheat; pulses are grams, peas, beans.

dw.Grains: Grains are rice, wheat, jowar, maize and ragi.
dw.Pulses: Pulses are grams, peas and beans.
dw.Cereals: Cereals are grains such as rice and wheat.

bank.q: On which bases are seeds classified in the slides?
bank.a: Number of cotyledons, endosperm, storage, type of food
d: Fruit type, flower type, leaf type
bank.why: Seeds are classified by number of cotyledons, endosperm (albuminous or not), storage (orthodox or recalcitrant) and type of food.

dw.Color, size, shape, weight: Color, size, shape and weight are not the bases used.
dw.Fruit type, flower type, leaf type: Fruit, flower and leaf type are not the bases used.
dw.Pollination, dispersal, germination: Pollination, dispersal and germination are not the bases used.

bank.q: In the monocot (corn) seed diagram, which structure fills most of the seed?
bank.why: Dicot seeds store food in the two cotyledons instead.

dw.Cotyledons: In corn, the endosperm is the large food store.
dw.Epicotyl: The epicotyl is the embryonic shoot.
dw.Radicle: The radicle is the embryonic root.

bank.q: A seed bank dries a batch of mango seeds to 10% moisture to store them, but almost none germinate afterward. Why?
bank.a: Mango seeds are recalcitrant and cannot survive desiccation
d: Mango seeds are orthodox and needed to be dried even further
Mango seeds lack an embryo, so they can never germinate
Mango seeds are albuminous, so drying spoils their endosperm
bank.why: Recalcitrant seeds die when dried to low moisture.

dw.Mango seeds are orthodox and needed to b: Mango seeds are recalcitrant, not orthodox.
dw.Mango seeds are albuminous, so drying sp: The problem is the drying, which a recalcitrant seed cannot tolerate.

bank.q: Chili (Capsicum annuum) seeds dried to below 10% moisture still germinate well after a year at sub-freezing temperature. What type of seeds are they?
bank.why: Orthodox seeds survive drying and freezing.

dw.Viviparous: Viviparous means germinating on the parent plant.

bank.q: A corn seedling grows, but its cotyledon stays below the soil surface. What type of germination is this?
bank.why: Monocots usually show hypogeal germination.

dw.Epigeal: Epigeal means the cotyledons rise above the soil.
dw.Viviparous: Viviparous means germinating on the parent plant.
dw.Delayed: Delayed is not a type of germination taught.

bank.q: A bean seedling pushes its two cotyledons above the soil as it grows. What type of germination is this?
bank.why: Dicots usually show epigeal germination.

dw.Hypogeal: Hypogeal means the cotyledons stay below the soil.
dw.Viviparous: Viviparous means germinating on the parent plant.

bank.q: When a pea seed is opened, there is no separate endosperm; its food is stored in two large cotyledons. How is the seed classified?
bank.why: Pea: two cotyledons, no endosperm.

dw.Albuminous monocot seed: Peas have two cotyledons (dicot) and no endosperm.
dw.Albuminous dicot seed: Peas have no endosperm, so they are not albuminous.
dw.Exalbuminous monocot seed: Peas have two cotyledons, so they are not monocots.

bank.q: A seed lot germinates well, but it is mixed with weed seeds and bits of soil. Which characteristic of a good seed does it fail?
bank.why: Good seed must be pure and free from inert materials and weed seeds.

dw.Viability: The seeds germinate well, so viability is fine.
dw.Being true to type: The problem is the mixing, not the variety.
dw.Uniformity of structure: Uniformity of structure is not the issue.

bank.q: A clean, disease-free seed lot looks uniform, but most seeds fail to germinate. Which characteristic does it fail?
bank.why: Good seeds must be viable with tested germination capacity.

dw.Purity: The lot is clean, so purity is fine.

bank.q: Plants grown from a seed lot look different from the variety printed on the packet. Which characteristic of a good seed does it fail?
bank.why: True to type: the plants match the variety named. Purity is about inert matter and weed seeds; viability is about germination.

dw.Purity: Mixed weeds are a purity problem, not variety.
dw.Uniformity: Uniformity is about structure and texture.

bank.q: A farmer stores coffee seeds in a freezer to keep them for next year, but they fail to germinate. What is the most likely reason?
bank.a: Coffee seeds are recalcitrant and sensitive to chilling or freezing
d: Coffee seeds are orthodox and needed to be dried before freezing
Coffee seeds have no endosperm, so they cannot store any food
Coffee seeds need epigeal germination, which freezing prevents
bank.why: Coffee seeds are recalcitrant: they die when dried and are sensitive to chilling, so freezing kills them. Orthodox seeds can be frozen.

dw.Coffee seeds are orthodox and needed to: Coffee seeds are recalcitrant, not orthodox.
dw.Coffee seeds have no endosperm, so they: Coffee seeds are not described as lacking stored food.
dw.Coffee seeds need epigeal germination, w: Epigeal germination is not why freezing fails.

bank.q: A researcher wants to find out whether a new seed is orthodox or recalcitrant. What is the best design?
bank.a: Split one seed lot: dry part of it to 10% moisture or less and store it below freezing, keep the rest fresh, then compare the germination of both
d: Plant all the fresh seeds right away and count the seedlings; a high germination rate means the seed is orthodox
Dry the new seeds and some mango seeds to 10% moisture, store both frozen, and compare their germination
Dry all the seeds to 10% moisture, freeze them for a year, and check germination with no undried group kept
bank.why: Same lot; only the drying and freezing differ.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

dw.Plant all the fresh seeds right away and: Fresh germination alone cannot show drying and freezing tolerance.
dw.Dry the new seeds and some mango seeds t: That compares two species instead of treated and untreated seeds of the same lot.
dw.Dry all the seeds to 10% moisture, freez: With no undried group there is no control for comparison.

bank.q: A student wants to test whether the endosperm of corn feeds the young seedling. Which design is best?
bank.a: Carefully remove the endosperm from some corn grains and leave others whole, germinate all in the same conditions, and compare seedling growth
d: Grow corn and beans side by side in the same soil and compare which seedlings grow faster in the first week
Remove the endosperm from all the corn grains, germinate them, and check whether any seedlings survive
Soak some corn grains for one hour and others for a day, then compare how quickly the seedlings grow
bank.why: Only the endosperm differs.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

dw.Grow corn and beans side by side in the: Corn and beans differ in many ways, not just endosperm.
dw.Remove the endosperm from all the corn g: With no intact group there is no control.
dw.Soak some corn grains for one hour and o: Soaking time tests water uptake, not the endosperm.

bank.q: Before selling a seed lot, a seed company wants to know its germination capacity. What should it do?
bank.a: Take random samples from the lot, germinate them in standard conditions in several replicates, and count the percentage that germinate
d: Plant the whole lot in one field and count the plants that come up after a month of whatever weather follows
Pick out the biggest and healthiest-looking seeds, germinate them, and report that percentage for the lot
Germinate one handful of seeds once in a warm room and report the percentage that sprout for the whole lot
bank.why: Random samples + replicates give a fair estimate of viability.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

dw.Plant the whole lot in one field and cou: One field after a month of weather is not a standard test.
dw.Pick out the biggest and healthiest-look: Picking the best seeds biases the result.
dw.Germinate one handful of seeds once in a: One handful once is not enough replication.

bank.q: A flower has petals, stamens and carpels, but no sepals ever form. How is it classified?
bank.why: Any missing whorl makes a flower incomplete.

dw.Complete flower: A complete flower has all four whorls.
dw.Unisexual flower: Unisexual means only one reproductive whorl is present; this flower has both.
dw.Petaloid flower: Petaloid describes a colorful calyx, and there is no calyx here.

bank.q: A gardener removes all the anthers from a bisexual flower before they open. The flower now works like which type?
bank.why: Only the gynoecium is left functioning.

dw.Staminate (male) flower: Without anthers it cannot make pollen, so it is not male.
dw.Complete bisexual flower: It lost the parts of a whorl, so it is no longer a complete bisexual flower.
dw.Apetalous flower: Removing anthers does not affect the petals.

bank.q: A fruit forms from the ovary but also includes the fleshy receptacle and other flower parts, like a pineapple. What is it called?
bank.why: Ovary + other flower parts = accessory fruit.

dw.True fruit: A true fruit is from the ovary only.
dw.Simple dry fruit: A simple dry fruit has a dry wall; the pineapple is fleshy.
dw.Schizocarp: A schizocarp is a dry, splitting fruit.

bank.q: A small fruit has a thin skin, and its whole ovary wall is soft and juicy around several seeds, with no stony pit. What type is it?
bank.why: Juicy ovary wall and no stone = berry (grape).

dw.Drupe: A drupe has a stony pit.
dw.Nut: A nut is a dry, hard fruit.

bank.q: A mustard plant forms long, slender dry pods; each opens into two valves, leaving the seeds on a central partition. What type of fruit is it?
bank.why: Long and slender, 2 carpels = silique.

dw.Silicle: A silicle is short and broad.

bank.term: Splits through the middle of each chamber
bank.q: A lily fruit from three carpels splits lengthwise along the middle of each chamber's outer wall. What type of capsule is it?
bank.why: Splitting along the outer median line = loculicidal.

dw.Septicidal capsule: Septicidal capsules split along the septa.

bank.q: A capsule of several carpels splits along the partitions between its chambers and opens at the top. What type is it?
bank.why: Splitting along the septa = septicidal (Dutchman's pipe).

dw.Loculicidal capsule: Loculicidal capsules split along the outer median line.
dw.Pyxis: A pyxis opens like a lid.

bank.term: Big food store outside the embryo
bank.q: When a castor seed is cut open, a large food tissue surrounds the embryo outside its cotyledons. How is the seed classified?
bank.why: Castor seeds have endosperm.

bank.q: An onion seedling, a monocot, lifts its cotyledon above the soil as it germinates. What does this show?
bank.a: Onion is the exception: its germination is epigeal
bank.why: Monocots are usually hypogeal, except onion.

dw.All monocots germinate epigeally: Onion is the exception, so not all monocots germinate epigeally.
dw.The seed is recalcitrant: Recalcitrance is about storage, not germination.

bank.q: A student wants to test whether the calyx protects the flower bud before it opens. Which design is best?
bank.a: Remove the sepals from some buds and leave others intact on the same plants, keep all in the same conditions, and compare bud damage
d: Remove the sepals from every bud on one plant and compare it with a different plant left untouched
Count the sepals on buds of several species and compare which species have fewer damaged buds
Remove the petals from some buds and leave others intact, then compare bud damage over a week
bank.why: Same plants and conditions; only the sepals differ.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

dw.Remove the sepals from every bud on one: Comparing two plants adds plant differences.
dw.Count the sepals on buds of several spec: Counting sepals across species compares species, not the effect of the calyx.
dw.Remove the petals from some buds and lea: Removing petals tests the petals, not the calyx.

bank.q: A researcher wants to test whether bean pods must dry out before they split open. What is the best design?
bank.a: Pick mature pods from the same plants, keep half in a humid chamber and let half dry in open air at the same temperature, then count how many split
d: Pick mature pods from the same plants, keep all of them in a humid chamber at the same temperature, then count how many split
Keep bean pods to dry in open air and pea pods in a humid chamber at the same temperature, then count how many split
Dry half the pods in a hot oven and leave the other half on the plant outdoors, then count how many split
bank.why: Same pods and temperature; only humidity differs.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

dw.Pick mature pods from the same plants, k: With no drying group there is nothing to compare.
dw.Keep bean pods to dry in open air and pe: Bean and pea are different species.
dw.Dry half the pods in a hot oven and leav: A hot oven changes the temperature too.

bank.term: Experiment: seed coat protects the embryo
bank.q: A student wants to test whether the seed coat protects the embryo from fungal attack. Which design is best?
bank.a: Peel the seed coat from some seeds of one lot and leave others whole, place all on the same moist, fungus-exposed medium, and compare how many rot
d: Peel the seed coat from all the seeds of one lot, place them on the same moist, fungus-exposed medium, and count how many rot
Peel the seed coat from some bean seeds and leave corn grains whole, place all on the same moist medium, and compare
Peel some seeds and leave others whole, but put the whole ones on a sterile medium and the peeled on a fungus-exposed one
bank.why: Same seed lot and medium; only the seed coat differs.
bank.hint: Change one thing; keep a control.

dw.Peel the seed coat from all the seeds of: Peeling all the seeds leaves no control group.
dw.Peel the seed coat from some bean seeds: Bean and corn are different species, so more than the coat differs.
dw.Peel some seeds and leave others whole,: Using different media changes more than the seed coat.

bank.q: Plants are producers. Which process do they use to make their own food?
bank.why: Plants are producers and use photosynthesis to make food.

dw.Fermentation: Fermentation is how yeast gets energy without oxygen.
dw.Chemosynthesis: Chemosynthesis uses chemicals, not light; plants use light.
dw.Digestion: Digestion breaks down food that was already made.

bank.q: Which statement is true of ALL plants?
bank.a: They have eukaryotic cells with cell walls
d: They have prokaryotic cells without a nucleus
They get food by eating other organisms
bank.why: All plants are producers with eukaryotic cells and cell walls, and they have a cuticle. Seeds in fruits are only for angiosperms.

dw.They have prokaryotic cells without a nu: Plant cells are eukaryotic, with a nucleus.
dw.They get food by eating other organisms: Plants make their own food; they do not eat.
dw.They form seeds inside fruits: Only angiosperms form seeds inside fruits.

bank.q: Which protective outer covering do all plants have, according to the lesson?
bank.why: All plants share three characteristics: producers, eukaryotic cells with walls, and a cuticle.

dw.A shell: A shell is not a plant covering.
dw.A fruit wall: A fruit wall belongs only to angiosperms.
dw.A layer of scales: Scales are not a plant covering shared by all plants.

bank.q: The tiny duckweed grows to about 10 mm. About how tall does the giant redwood grow?
bank.why: Plants range from duckweed (about 10 mm) to the giant redwood (about 100 m).

dw.About 10 m: 10 m is far too short for a giant redwood.

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the criteria used to classify the plant kingdom into subgroups?
d: Whether the plant body is well differentiated
Whether there is a vascular system
Whether seeds are formed, and how
bank.why: The three criteria are plant body, vascular system and seed formation (flowers and seeds, naked or in a fruit).

dw.Whether the plant body is well different: The body is one of the three criteria.
dw.Whether there is a vascular system: The vascular system is one of the three criteria.
dw.Whether seeds are formed, and how: Seed formation is one of the three criteria.

bank.q: A well-differentiated plant body is one that has...
bank.why: Body differentiation means roots, stems and leaves.

dw.Only a thallus: A thallus is a body that is not differentiated.
dw.Flowers and fruits: Flowers and fruits are reproductive structures, not body parts.
dw.Spores and sporangia: Spores and sporangia are reproductive structures.

bank.q: Which tissues make up the vascular system that carries water and other substances?
bank.why: The vascular system is xylem and phloem.

dw.Cuticle and epidermis: The cuticle and epidermis are dermal tissue.
dw.Cortex and pith: The cortex and pith are ground tissue.
dw.Cambium and cork: The cambium makes new tissue and cork is protective.

bank.q: When classifying by seed formation, the lesson asks whether the seeds are...
bank.a: Naked or enclosed in a fruit
d: Smooth or rough on the coat
bank.why: Seed formation: presence or absence of flowers and seeds, and whether seeds are naked or enclosed in a fruit.

dw.Large or small at maturity: Size is not the seed criterion.
dw.Smooth or rough on the coat: Surface texture is not the seed criterion.
dw.Winged or wingless for dispersal: Wings are not the seed criterion.

bank.q: Plants that have no vascular tissue are called...
bank.why: Nonvascular plants are the mosses and liverworts.

dw.Seedless vascular plants: Seedless vascular plants have xylem and phloem.

bank.q: Which pair belongs to the nonvascular plants?
bank.why: Mosses and liverworts are small, simple plants that live in moist places.

dw.Conifers and cycads: Conifers and cycads are vascular seed plants.
dw.Roses and mangoes: Roses and mangoes are vascular flowering plants.

bank.q: Vascular plants are divided into which two groups?
bank.why: Vascular plants are those that produce seeds and those that do not.

dw.Flowering and non-flowering plants: Flowering and non-flowering splits the seed plants, not the vascular plants.
dw.Monocots and dicots: Monocots and dicots are angiosperm classes.
dw.Land and aquatic plants: Land and aquatic is not the split used.

bank.q: Seed plants are divided into...
bank.why: Gymnosperms have seeds in cones; angiosperms have seeds in fruits.

dw.Monocots and thallophytes: Monocots belong to angiosperms; thallophytes are cryptogams.
dw.Cryptogams and algae: Cryptogams and algae are not the seed plant groups.

bank.q: Which plants are seedless vascular plants?
bank.why: Seedless vascular plants include ferns, club mosses and horsetails.

bank.q: A seed is a structure that contains...
bank.a: A plant embryo and a food supply inside a protective covering
d: A spore and a sperm cell enclosed in a thin film of water
An ovary and an ovule enclosed inside the petals of a flower
A rhizoid and a frond enclosed inside the wall of a fruit
bank.why: A seed holds an embryo plus food in a protective covering.

dw.A spore and a sperm cell enclosed in a t: A spore and a sperm are not a seed.
dw.An ovary and an ovule enclosed inside th: An ovary and an ovule are flower parts.
dw.A rhizoid and a frond enclosed inside th: A rhizoid and a frond are not seed parts.

bank.q: Cryptogams are plants that are...
bank.why: Cryptogams are non-flowering and non-seed bearing; phanerogams are flowering and seed bearing.

dw.Flowering but seedless: Flowering but seedless is not a plant group.
dw.Seed bearing but non-flowering: Seed bearing plants without flowers are gymnosperms, which are phanerogams.

bank.q: Phanerogams are plants that are...
bank.why: Phanerogams are the flowering, seed-bearing plants.

dw.Non-flowering but seed bearing: Non-flowering seed bearing plants (gymnosperms) are also phanerogams, but 'flowering and seed bearing' is the definition.

bank.q: By the lesson's criteria, the plant kingdom is classified into how many subgroups?
bank.why: Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Gymnosperms and Angiosperms.

dw.Three: Three is too few; there are five subgroups.

bank.q: Which three groups are the cryptogams?
bank.why: Cryptogams: Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta. Phanerogams: Gymnosperms and Angiosperms.

bank.q: Which two groups are the phanerogams?
bank.why: The phanerogams bear seeds: naked (gymnosperms) or enclosed in fruit (angiosperms).

dw.Pteridophyta and Gymnosperms: Pteridophyta is a cryptogam; gymnosperms make seeds.

bank.q: Organisms of the Kingdom Plantae are typically...
bank.why: Plants are eukaryotic, multicellular and autotrophic.

bank.q: The rigid plant cell wall is made of...
bank.why: Plant cell walls are cellulose.

dw.Keratin: Keratin is in animal hair and nails.

bank.q: What does the plant cell wall give the plant?
bank.a: Strength, shape and support for upright growth
d: The ability to move toward sources of food
A protective place to store the nucleus
The power to engulf other cells whole
bank.why: The wall gives structural strength, protection and support for upright growth on land.

dw.The ability to move toward sources of fo: Plants do not move toward food.
dw.A protective place to store the nucleus: The nucleus is not stored in the wall.
dw.The power to engulf other cells whole: Plant cells do not engulf other cells.

bank.q: Which green pigment in chloroplasts captures light for photosynthesis?
bank.why: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which converts light energy into chemical energy.

dw.Keratin: Keratin is a protein in hair and nails.

bank.q: Sofia finds a green organism whose cells have a nucleus, a cellulose wall and chloroplasts, and it makes its own food. Which kingdom does it belong to?
bank.why: Eukaryotic, cellulose wall, chloroplasts and autotrophic means Kingdom Plantae.

dw.Animalia: Animals have no cell walls or chloroplasts.
dw.Bacteria: Bacteria are prokaryotic and have no nucleus.

bank.term: Why it is not a plant
bank.q: A scientist finds an organism with no cell wall that gets food by eating other organisms. Why can it NOT be a plant?
bank.a: Plants are producers with cell walls
d: Plants never have a nucleus in any cell
Plants must be microscopic in size
Plants always form seeds in a fruit
bank.why: Plants make their own food and have cell walls.

bank.q: Carlo says tiny duckweed and giant redwood cannot be in the same kingdom. Which characteristic shows both are plants?
bank.a: Both make food by photosynthesis and have cell walls
d: Both reach about the same height at maturity
Both bear their seeds in cones on branches
Both lack xylem and phloem in their bodies
bank.why: Size does not matter: all plants are producers with eukaryotic cells and cell walls.

dw.Both reach about the same height at matu: Duckweed and redwood differ greatly in height.

bank.q: A botanist records a plant with xylem and phloem, leafy fronds and no seeds. Which group is it?
bank.why: Vascular tissue and no seeds point to seedless vascular plants such as ferns.

dw.Nonvascular plants without seeds: Nonvascular plants have no xylem or phloem.

bank.q: A student finds a small green plant on a damp rock. It has no xylem or phloem. Which group is it?
bank.why: No vascular tissue plus a moist habitat points to the nonvascular plants.

dw.Seedless vascular plants: It lacks xylem and phloem, so it is not seedless vascular.
dw.Gymnosperms: Gymnosperms are vascular and bear seeds.
dw.Angiosperms: Angiosperms are vascular and bear seeds.

bank.q: A tree bears its seeds in cones and does not make flowers or fruits. Which group is it?
bank.why: Gymnosperms have seeds housed in cones.

bank.q: Mara keys out a plant with a well-differentiated body, a vascular system and seeds enclosed in a fruit. Which group is it?
bank.why: Seeds enclosed in a fruit mark the angiosperms.

dw.Bryophyta: Bryophytes have no seeds or vascular tissue.

bank.q: A plant has a vascular system but never makes flowers or seeds. Which term fits it?
bank.why: Non-flowering, non-seed-bearing plants are cryptogams.

dw.A phanerogam: Phanerogams are flowering and seed bearing.
dw.An angiosperm: Angiosperms are flowering and seed bearing.

bank.q: A sorting key first asks, 'Does the plant have vascular tissue?' Which two plants does this question separate?
bank.why: Mosses are nonvascular; ferns are vascular.

bank.q: Thallophyta are primitive plants whose body is NOT differentiated into...
bank.why: Thallophytes lack well-differentiated roots, stems and leaves.

dw.Cells and tissues: Thallophytes do have cells and tissues.
dw.Cell walls and nuclei: Thallophytes have cell walls and nuclei.

bank.q: The simple, undifferentiated body of a thallophyte is called a...
bank.why: Thallus: a body that is not divided into root, stem and leaves.

dw.Frond: A frond is a fern leaf.
dw.Rhizome: A rhizome is a fern stem.
dw.Protonema: A protonema starts a moss gametophyte.

bank.q: Most thallophytes live in...
bank.why: They lack true roots and vascular tissue, so they live in water or damp places.

dw.Hot, dry deserts: Deserts are too dry for thallophytes.
dw.Open sunny fields: Dry sunny fields are too dry.
dw.Snow-covered land: Snow-covered land is not their habitat.

bank.q: Which thallophyte has a filamentous (thread-like) body?
bank.why: Spirogyra and Ulothrix are filamentous; Volvox is colonial.

bank.q: Volvox is best described as a...
bank.why: Volvox: colonial (groups of cells living together).

dw.Filamentous green alga: Spirogyra is the filamentous green alga.

bank.q: Fucus is a...
bank.why: Fucus is the brown alga in the lesson's list.

dw.Green alga: Spirogyra and Volvox are green algae.
dw.Moss: A moss is a bryophyte, not an alga.

bank.q: Polysiphonia is a...
bank.why: Polysiphonia is a red alga.

dw.Green alga: Volvox and Ulva are green algae.

bank.q: Which thallophyte is called the sea lettuce?
bank.why: Ulva is a flat, leaf-like green alga that is used as food.

dw.Chara: Chara is a green, plant-like alga.
dw.Cladophora: Cladophora is a branched filamentous alga.

bank.q: Which thallophyte is a branched filamentous alga?
bank.why: Cladophora is branched and filamentous.

bank.q: Most thallophytes (the algae) get their food by...
bank.why: Algae are autotrophic. Some members, such as fungi, are heterotrophic.

dw.Eating other organisms: Algae make their own food; eating is not their way.
dw.Absorbing dead matter only: Absorbing dead matter describes fungi, not algae.

bank.q: The reserve food of thallophytes is generally...
bank.why: Excess glucose is stored as starch.

dw.Glycogen: Glycogen is the storage of animals.
dw.Oil: Oil is not the usual reserve.
dw.Protein: Protein is not the usual reserve.

bank.q: The cell wall of a thallophyte is made of...
bank.why: Cellulose gives the cells rigidity and protection.

dw.Lignin: Lignin is in the walls of vascular plants.
dw.Keratin: Keratin is a protein of animals.

bank.q: Thallophytes stay small and live in wet places mainly because they lack...
bank.why: No vascular tissue, so they absorb water and nutrients straight from the surroundings.

bank.q: How do thallophytes take in water and nutrients?
bank.a: Directly from the surroundings through the body surface
d: Through true roots that carry water up into the whole body
Through xylem vessels that run along the length of the thallus
Through an underground rhizome that stores water for the plant
bank.why: They have no roots or vascular tissue.

bank.q: The sex organs of thallophytes are...
bank.why: Simple, single-celled sex organs.

dw.Multicellular with a protective jacket: Jacketed multicellular organs belong to higher plants.

bank.q: What does NOT form after fertilization in a thallophyte, unlike in higher plants?
bank.why: No embryo formation is a key feature of thallophytes.

bank.q: Agar is an industrial product made from which thallophytes?
bank.why: Red algae give agar; Ulva is eaten as food.

dw.Brown algae: Brown algae are not the agar source.

bank.q: A student finds a leaf with parallel veins on a plant with fibrous roots and one-cotyledon seeds. Which group is it?
bank.why: Parallel veins, adventitious roots and one cotyledon are monocot traits.

dw.Dicot: Dicots have netted veins and two cotyledons.
dw.Gymnosperm: Gymnosperms have no flowers or broad veined leaves.

bank.q: A plant has a taproot, netted leaf veins and flowers with five petals. How is it classified?
bank.why: Taproot, reticulate venation and floral parts in fives mean dicot.

bank.q: A stem cross section shows vascular bundles arranged in a ring. Which kind of plant is it from?
bank.why: Ring arrangement is typical of dicots.

bank.q: Kai says every seed plant must bloom. Which example corrects him?
bank.a: Gymnosperms bear naked seeds in cones without flowers
d: Ferns bear seeds in their sporangia on the fronds
Mosses bear seeds in the capsules of the sporophyte
Algae bear seeds in the thallus of the plant body
bank.why: Seed plants include gymnosperms, which have no flowers.

bank.q: Which comparison of a pine tree and an apple tree is correct?
bank.a: Pine seeds are naked; apple seeds are enclosed in a fruit
d: Pine seeds are enclosed in a fruit; apple seeds are naked
Both trees enclose their seeds in a fruit
bank.why: Pine = gymnosperm; apple = angiosperm.

dw.Pine seeds are enclosed in a fruit; appl: The pine's seeds are naked, and the apple's are enclosed.
dw.Both trees enclose their seeds in a frui: Only the apple encloses its seeds in a fruit.

bank.q: A fruit is cut open and its seeds are found inside. Which group of seed plants produced it?
bank.why: Seeds enclosed in fruits mean angiosperms.

bank.q: A lily flower has its parts in threes, and its leaves have parallel veins. Which class is it?
bank.why: Floral parts in threes and parallel veins are monocot traits.

dw.Dicot: Lilies have parts in threes and parallel veins.

bank.q: A conifer drops woody cones, and the seeds sit unprotected on the cone scales. Which description fits?
d: Angiosperm, with seeds in a fruit

notes: Meristems by origin

Promeristem — earliest, embryonic, made of initials; makes primary meristems | Primary meristem — primary tissues → length | Secondary meristem — from permanent cells that divide again → thickness (vascular and cork cambium)
Meristems by position
Apical — tips → length (primary growth) | Intercalary — base of leaves, nodes, internodes → length; grass regrows after mowing | Lateral — sides → girth (secondary growth); vascular + cork cambium
Primary meristems
Protoderm — epidermis | Ground meristem — cortex and pith | Procambium — primary xylem and phloem
Meristem cells
Living, thin-walled | Few small vacuoles | Dense protoplasm, conspicuous nuclei | Spherical, oval, polygonal | No reserve food
Simple tissues

Parenchyma — most abundant; living, thin wall, big vacuole; photosynthesis, storage, wound healing | Chlorenchyma — chloroplasts, photosynthesis | Aerenchyma — air spaces, buoyancy | Collenchyma — kolla 'glue'; living, uneven thick wall, below epidermis; flexible support | Sclerenchyma — skleros 'hard'; lignin, dead; rigid support | Fibers — long, bend in wind | Sclereids — stone cells, rock-hard
Dermal tissue

Derma — skin | Epidermis — one layer, closely packed | Periderm — replaces epidermis in older woody parts; dead cork cells | Trichomes — hairs vs herbivores (nettle: histamine) | Cuticle — cutin; prevents water loss | Guard cells — chloroplasts; form stomata for gas exchange
Vascular tissue
Tracheophyta — vascular plants | Main function — conduction; also support | Sap — contents of xylem and phloem | Xylem — water and minerals up | Phloem — food from leaves (source → sink)
Xylem cells
Tracheids — long, tapered, dead; pits; torus valve | Vessels (trachea) — wider, shorter; perforation plates | Xylem fibers — support | Xylem parenchyma — only living; stores ergastic substances
Phloem cells

Sieve-tube elements — living, no nucleus; sieve plates | Companion cells — nucleus; supply proteins; plasmodesmata | Phloem parenchyma — stores starch | Phloem fibers — support | Primary phloem — procambium | Secondary phloem — vascular cambium
Ground tissue
Also called — fundamental tissue system | Cortex — between dermal and vascular | Pith — inside vascular tissue
Root characteristics
Descending, non-green | No nodes, internodes, leaves, buds | Root cap = calyptra | + hydrotropic, − phototropic, + geotropic | Radial bundles, exarch xylem | Unicellular root hairs
Root systems
Tap root — from the radicle; one deep main root; dicots | Adventitious — from stem, leaf, hypocotyl; many equal roots; surface feeders; monocots
Zones (tip upward)

Root cap — protects; starch senses gravity; Golgi → mucilage | Meristematic — ~1 mm; division; calyptrogen (apex), histogen (base) | Elongation — 4–8 mm; vacuolization | Root hair — piliferous; main absorption; ephemeral | Maturation — bulk; lateral roots; secondary growth
Root cap special cases
Root pockets — Eichhornia, Pistia, Lemna | Multiple root caps — Pandanus | Reduced or absent — mycorrhizal roots
Root function examples

Storage — carrot, radish | Extra support — banyan, maize | Aeration — mangroves | Reproduction — dahlia | Floating — Jussiaea | Photosynthesis — Tinospora | Nitrogen fixation — pea | Food from host — Cuscuta | Water from air — Vanda | Climbing — Pothos | Phosphates — mycorrhiza | Green roots — Trapa

Conical — carrot | Fusiform — radish (spindle) | Napiform — turnip (spherical top) | Tuberous — Mirabilis (no shape)
Adventitious modifications
Tuberous — sweet potato (starch) | Fasciculated — dahlia (inulin) | Moniliform — beaded | Nodulose — swollen tips | Annulated — rings | Stilt — sugarcane, maize | Palmate — hand-like
Mangroves
Halophytes in salty waterlogged mud | Pneumatophores — breathing roots, grow up, lenticels; Avicennia, Sonneratia | Stilt roots — Rhizophora | Vivipary — seeds germinate on the parent
Roots and microbes

Rhizosphere — soil around the root | Rhizoplane — root surface | PGPR — growth-promoting rhizobacteria | Ectotrophic mycorrhiza — outside sheath; Pinus, Eucalyptus, oak | Endotrophic — inside cortex; vesicles (lipids), arbuscules; VAM → phosphate
Stem basics
Central axis | From the epicotyl | Phototropic | Branches in leaf axils | Nodes, internodes, buds
External parts

Terminal bud — auxin suppresses lateral buds (apical dominance) | Lateral bud — leaf axil | Bud scale — modified leaf | Leaf scar — where a leaf fell | Bundle scar — inside the leaf scar; identifies woody plants | Lenticel — gas exchange pores | Bark — protective, develops with age
Texture
Herbaceous — banana; no wood, dies after flowering | Suffrutescent — eggplant, jute; woody base | Woody — trees, shrubs; secondary xylem
Underground stems

Rhizome — horizontal; ginger, turmeric | Tuber — swollen tip of underground branch; eyes; potato | Bulb — disc stem, fleshy leaves; onion, garlic (tunicated) | Corm — solid swollen base; Colocasia, Amorphophallus
Subaerial stems
Runner — along soil; Oxalis, strawberry, Centella | Offset — short, thick; Pistia, Eichhornia | Stolon — underground then up at the tip; Colocasia | Sucker — underground then turns up; Chrysanthemum
Aerial stems

Stem tendril — Cissus (terminal bud), passion fruit (axillary bud) | Stem thorn — Duranta, Carissa, Citrus | Thorn = stem, spine = leaf, prickle = no vascular tissue | Phylloclade — flat green stem; Opuntia | Cladode — 1–2 internodes | Cladophyll — Asparagus | Bulbil — Agave (floral bud), Dioscorea (axillary bud)
Leaf basics
Lateral outgrowths of nodes | From leaf primordia (exogenous) | Heterophylly — different leaves on one plant (Limnophila: dissected underwater, entire in air)
Leaf parts

Hypopodium — leaf base | Mesopodium — stalk | Epipodium — lamina | Pulvinus — swollen base; Mimosa sleep movements | Sheathing base — monocots | Stipules — protect buds; stipulate vs exstipulate | Petiole (simple) vs rachis (compound) | Sessile — no stalk

Sheathing base | No petiole in grasses | Ligules | Isobilateral | Parallel venation
Venation
Reticulate — network; dicots | Parallel — monocots; horizontal (banana), longitudinal (bamboo) | Dicot exceptions — Calophyllum, Alstonia, Eryngium | Monocot exceptions — aroids, Dioscorea
Compound leaves

Paripinnate — even (tamarind) | Imparipinnate — odd (rose, neem) | Bipinnate — Acacia, Mimosa | Tripinnate — Moringa | Decompound — coriander | Unifoliate — Citrus | Trifoliate — rubber | Quadrifoliate — Marsilea | Multifoliate — Bombax, tapioca

Linear — grass | Lanceolate — broad near base | Oblanceolate — broad near apex | Ovate — egg | Obovate — inverted egg | Cordate — heart | Obcordate — inverted heart | Reniform — kidney | Sagittate — arrowhead | Falcate — sickle | Acicular — needle | Lorate — strap

Entire — smooth | Serrate — teeth point up | Dentate — teeth point out | Crenate — rounded teeth | Undulate — wavy | Acute — sharp | Acuminate — long tail | Obtuse — blunt | Cuspidate — spiny point | Mucronate — short point | Retuse — shallow notch | Emarginate — deep notch

Purpose — light | Prefoliation, ptyxis, vernation — leaves in the bud | Radical — radish | Alternate — 1 per node (spiral, distichous, tristichous) | Opposite — decussate (right angles), superposed (stacked) | Whorled — 3+ (Nerium)

The flower

Flower — reproductive part; facilitates union of sperm and eggs | Smallest — Wolffia | Largest — Rafflesia | 4 whorls — calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium | Non-essential — calyx, corolla | Essential — androecium, gynoecium
Calyx and corolla

Calyx — outermost whorl; sepals; usually green | Petaloid — brightly colored calyx | Polysepalous — free sepals (rose) | Gamosepalous — fused sepals (Datura) | Corolla — 2nd whorl; petals; variously colored | Polypetalous — free petals (rose) | Gamopetalous — fused petals (Datura) | Apetalous — no petals (Brassica rapa)
Androecium and gynoecium

Androecium — 3rd whorl; male; stamens; pollen | Anther — head with pollen | Filament — stalk | Gynoecium — innermost; female; carpels; becomes the fruit | Stigma — sticky top | Style — tube to the ovary | Ovary — fertilization; eggs; ovary wall → fruit coat; ovules → seeds
Flower types

Complete — all 4 whorls; most bisexual flowers | Incomplete — any whorl missing; all unisexual flowers | Bisexual — androecium + gynoecium | Male = staminate — androecium only | Female = pistillate — gynoecium only
Fruit basics

Fruits — only in angiosperms | True fruit — ovary only | Accessory fruit — ovary + receptacle, petals, sepals (pineapple) | Simple — one ovary/pistil | Aggregate — many pistils, one flower | Multiple — pistils of many flowers (mulberry)
Fleshy fruits

Drupe — one seed, stony endocarp, fleshy mesocarp, thin exocarp; cherry, peach, plum, coconut (fibrous) | Berry — juicy ovary wall; grape, banana, gooseberry, tomato | Hesperidium — leathery rind, septa = carpels; orange, lemon | Pepo — hard rind; watermelon, squash, pumpkin, cucumber | Pome — accessory; core from ovary, pulp from perianth; 5+ carpels; apple, pear
Dry dehiscent fruits

Legume — 1 carpel, both sutures; pea, bean; peanut stays shut (ripens in soil) | Follicle — 1 carpel, one suture; larkspur, columbine, milkweed, Magnolia | Capsule — several carpels | Loculicidal — outer median line; lily, Viola | Poricidal — holes; poppy | Denticidal — teeth; corn cockle | Septicidal — along septa; Dutchman's pipe | Silique — long, 2 carpels; mustard | Silicle — short, broad | Pyxis — lid; plantain
Dry indehiscent fruits

Achene — one seed attached at one point; buttercup, dandelion, sunflower | Nut — very hard wall; oak (acorn), chestnut, hazel; cup = involucre | Samara — winged; elm, maple, ash | Grain (caryopsis) — seed coat fused to pericarp; wheat, corn | Schizocarp — splits into mericarps
Seeds
Seed — fertilized mature ovule + seed coat; propagating material | Parts — embryo, endosperm (stored food), seed coat (testa) | Good seed — true to type, pure, viable, uniform, disease-free
Seed types

Monocot — 1 cotyledon; wheat, corn, rice; hypogeal (not onion); adventitious roots; no secondary growth; endospermic | Dicot — 2 cotyledons; pea, bean, mango; epigeal (not pea, gram); non-endospermic; parts in 4s or 5s | Albuminous — endosperm; castor, poppy, custard apple | Exalbuminous — no endosperm; gram, pea, bean | Orthodox — survive drying/freezing; ≤10% moisture; Capsicum, Citrus, grains | Recalcitrant — die when dried; 30–70% moisture; coffee, mango, rubber, neem, jackfruit | Food — grains, pulses, oilseeds
Plant characteristics

All plants — producers (photosynthesis); eukaryotic cells with cellulose walls; cuticle | Kingdom Plantae — eukaryotic, multicellular, autotrophic; chloroplasts with chlorophyll | Sizes — duckweed ~10 mm to giant redwood ~100 m
Classifying plants

Criteria — plant body, vascular system, seed formation (naked or in a fruit) | Nonvascular — mosses, liverworts | Seedless vascular — ferns, club mosses, horsetails | Seed plants — gymnosperms, angiosperms | Seed — embryo + food in a protective covering
Cryptogams and phanerogams
Cryptogams — non-flowering, non-seed bearing: Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta | Phanerogams — flowering, seed bearing: Gymnosperms, Angiosperms | Five subgroups in all
Thallophyta

Thallus — no true roots, stems, leaves; no vascular tissue | Mostly aquatic; autotrophic (algae); fungi heterotrophic | Starch; cellulose wall; single-celled sex organs; no embryo | Volvox, Spirogyra, Ulothrix, Cladophora, Chara, Ulva, Fucus, Polysiphonia | Agar — red algae; Ulva — food
